catalogTitle: אצילות' ד' עולמות והשתלשלות איך עובדים ביחד. יש כמה מדריגות בנשמות אבל הנקודה של אברהם אבינו בכולם. נשמה ממדריגה נמוכה ביותר יכול להוליד נשמות גבוהות כי בתוכו מדריגת כתר. זה ענין מחול.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains how G-d's light descends through the four worlds and the levels of souls, and shows that beneath all the outer differences every Jew holds the same inner point from the Avos, which is revealed in the round dance and on Yom Kippur.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the ten sefiros, which match a person's ten powers of the soul and the ten utterances of Creation, and explains hishtalshelus, the descent of G-d's light, with a mashal of vapor turning into water and ice and of dark film used to watch an eclipse. The four worlds, Atzilus, Beriyah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, act as curtains, and each holds ten sefiros. Souls also come from these worlds, in some forty general levels, yet every Jew carries an inner point inherited from the Avos. With a mashal of coated aspirin and of inherited hair color he shows that the differences are only in the outer garments. Reading Tanya chapter 18, he explains that even the lowest Jew has chochmah within, because holiness is unity. From here he explains the round dance, machol, where all stand equally near Hashem, the mechilah of Yom Kippur, and the verse calling the Jews 'bnei kushiyim'.

en: G-d's light comes down through the four worlds, each acting as a curtain that dims it, so that the lower worlds and man can receive it.
Souls come from the four worlds in about forty general levels, from Chochmah of Atzilus down to Malchus of Asiyah, with countless finer levels within them.
Every Jew has an inner point inherited from the Avos, and in that point all Jews are equal; the differences between them are only in the outer garments.
Following Tanya chapter 18, even the lowest Jew, whose soul is nefesh of nefesh of Malchus of Asiyah, holds within him chochmah in which the light of Ein Sof shines.
Holiness is unity and impurity is division, so a Jew can connect to the Avos only when he is united with other Jews.
The round dance, machol, reveals the inner equality of all Jews, and the same revelation brings the mechilah of Yom Kippur.

candidateTopics: inner point inherited from the Avos

title.en: Ten sefiros and the descent of light

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the ten sefiros and the ten powers of the soul, links them to the ten utterances, ten plagues and ten commandments, and explains hishtalshelus with water turning from vapor to ice. He adds that creation cannot receive a light that is too strong, like the sun during an eclipse, which is watched through layers of dark film.

title.en: The four worlds as curtains

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the four worlds, matching the four letters of Hashem's name, and derives the name Atzilus from 'etzel', near, like the nobles near the king. Each world is a curtain that lets through only a little light, each holds ten sefiros, and together they form Hashem's reshus hayachid, ten high and four wide.

title.en: Levels of souls and the inner point

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that souls too come from the four worlds, from souls of Atzilus like Moshe Rabbeinu and the Avos down to the lowest level, nefesh of Malchus of Asiyah, in about forty general levels. Yet every Jew, even an am ha'aretz, has hidden within him the point he inherited from the Avos, and in it all are equal.

title.en: The mashal of the coated aspirin

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives a long mashal of an aspirin with a sweet coating over an enteric coating, so that it passes the mouth and the stomach unharmed and acts only in the intestines; under both coatings it is still aspirin. So too every Jew's inner point from the Avos is the same under coarse or refined garments, and he adds a mashal of hair color hidden in one generation and revealed in the next.

title.en: Tanya ch. 18: chochmah in the lowest Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter 18: the Avos are the merkavah and drew down nefesh, ruach and neshamah to their children from the four worlds, and even the lowest Jew has nefesh of nefesh of Malchus of Asiyah. Because in holiness all is unity, unlike the division of the sitra achra, this lowest level contains chochmah and the light of Ein Sof, as in 'Hashem bechochmah yasad aretz'.

title.en: The round dance of the tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara at the end of Taanis that Hashem will make a dance, machol, for the tzaddikim, and explains with the Chasam Sofer that in a round dance, as at a round table, everyone is equal and equally near Hashem in the center. Therefore a chassidic dance is a high avodah, one must not talk during it, and the dancers must hold hands like an unbroken electric circuit, as the Baal Shem Tov did.

title.en: Machol, mechilah and bnei kushiyim

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects machol with mechilah: on Yom Kippur the inner point of every Jew is revealed, and that is why he is forgiven. He then explains the verse calling the Jews 'bnei kushiyim': as with skin color, the difference is only on the surface, and beneath it every Jewish soul is a part of G-d above. He closes by noting that the next chapter of Tanya builds on this introduction.

catalogTitle: טעם שאפי' פושעים מולידים נשמות גדולות. חכמה למעלה מהשגה. פילפולי התורה מבינים אבל גזירות אינם מבינים. חכמה מקור הבינה. יארצייט המגיד ממזריטש זצוקללה”ה שהוא מקור החסידות.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 18, the Mashgiach explains why great souls are often born to simple Jews, why the darkest times bring the light of Moshiach as Chanukah does, and why chochmah, the source of binah, is beyond understanding.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter 18: even the lowest Jew has in his inwardness the highest level, and great souls are born even to simple people, as the Sefer HaGilgulim says. He explains that the hidden inheritance of the Avos surfaces in later generations, and that Hashem hides great souls among simple or sinful parents to outwit the Satan, as seen in the lineage of David HaMelech and a Midrash about Esav and David. He connects this to Chanukah, which falls in Teves, the hardest month and the longest night, and reveals a spark of the light of Moshiach, as will happen in the darkness of ikvesa dimeshicha. Today's trials are great, but like a stone dropped from high that sinks deep, today's souls fell from high places. Returning to Tanya, he explains through a river's hidden spring and an inventor who cannot explain gravity that chochmah is the source of binah and cannot be grasped. He closes with the yahrzeit of the Maggid of Mezritch.

en: Even the lowest Jew carries in his inwardness the highest levels, the inheritance of Avraham Avinu, which can surface in his children or grandchildren.
Hashem brings great souls through simple or sinful parents to outwit the Satan, who would never think to look there.
Chanukah comes at the lowest point of the year, in Teves and its longest night, and its lights reveal a spark of the light of Moshiach, just as Moshiach will be revealed in the lowest generation.
The souls of the generation before Moshiach fell from very high places and therefore sank deep, so they can raise sparks that earlier generations could not reach.
Chochmah is the source of binah and is beyond grasp: one can understand and explain what is built on the first point, but not the point itself.

title.en: Why simple people have great children

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter 18, that even the lowest soul holds within it the highest level and that great souls are born to simple people. He explains that the hidden inheritance of the Avos surfaces in later generations, like a talent for niggun that skips a generation.

title.en: Outwitting the Satan: the line of David

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem uses this to trick the Satan, as seen in the lineage of David HaMelech. He brings a Midrash that the Satan hoped for a share through Esav and later through David, who was also 'admoni', and compares it to an owner who hides his diamonds where a thief will not look.

title.en: Chanukah in the darkest night

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Teves belongs to Esav and is the hardest month, and that its long night is the time the sitra achra rules. Chanukah comes precisely then and its lights reveal a spark of the light of Moshiach, just as Moshiach will be revealed in the darkness of ikvesa dimeshicha.

title.en: The stone that falls from high

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the great trials of today's generation and asks whether it is lacking for being so low. With the mashal of a stone dropped into mud from a roof, he explains that today's souls fell from high and can raise sparks earlier generations could not, which is why great souls are sometimes born to simple fathers.

title.en: Chochmah, the hidden source of binah

summary.en: The Mashgiach learns the Tanya's words that chochmah is the source of intellect and above understanding. He illustrates it with a river fed by a hidden spring, the pasuk of the river going out of Eden, an inventor who can explain his machine but not why things fall, and a pilpul whose starting point cannot itself be explained. He breaks off to continue after Chanukah, and closes by noting the yahrzeit of the Maggid, the source of all of Chassidus, with lechaim and a niggun.

catalogTitle: כח התורה: Torah Missiles

oneLiner.en: With a war looming at the start of Adar, the Mashgiach teaches through the Chasam Sofer that when troubles contradict each other the only protection is Torah, and that the Jewish people's real weapons are Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens on Rosh Chodesh Adar with a war about to break out, noting that Adar is a month of strong mazal for Jews and that they too must gather forces: malachim created by Torah, mitzvos and tefillah. He tells from the Chasam Sofer's diary, Sefer Hazikaron, how Napoleon's siege of Pressburg killed hundreds of gentiles but only one Jew, an informer, and compares the first Gulf War. He brings the Chasam Sofer's reading of the passuk about many troubles: the Gemara allows praying for only one trouble at a time, but when troubles contradict like a bee sting and a scorpion sting, one cannot pray for peace since war may begin the geulah. The answer is the 'shira', the Torah, which protects. Tehillim 149 shows that the Jews' war is fought with the mouth. Finally he explains why Achashverosh, and in his view Bush, came to power against the people's will: Hashem appointed them for His purpose.

en: Adar is a month of strong mazal for Jews, and just as an army gathers soldiers, Jews must gather forces of malachim created by Torah, mitzvos and tefillah.
In the Chasam Sofer's time, Napoleon's bombardment of Pressburg killed hundreds of gentiles but only one Jew, who had informed on the Chasam Sofer.
When two troubles contradict each other, like a bee sting and a scorpion sting, one cannot pray for either remedy; this is why one could not simply pray for peace in a war that may bring the geulah.
The Chasam Sofer's answer is 'the shira', meaning the Torah: learning Torah is the protection that works whatever the troubles.
The war's outcome is decided not by presidents and generals but by Jews learning, davening and saying Tehillim, whose weapon is the mouth.
Achashverosh became king by himself and not by election, to make clear that Hashem had appointed him for the miracle of Purim.

candidateTopics: prayer for one trouble at a time
war as the beginning of geulah
Torah, tefillah and tzedakah as weapons

title.en: A looming war and the mazal of Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens on Rosh Chodesh Adar with a war about to begin that no leader can predict. He brings the Gemara that a Jew in a dispute with a gentile should seek it in Adar, whose mazal is strong, and says that just as the American army gathers soldiers, Jews must gather malachim through Torah, mitzvos and tefillah.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer's diary of Napoleon's siege

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Chasam Sofer's Sefer Hazikaron, a diary of Napoleon's months-long siege of Pressburg: the signs he received beforehand, the yeshiva's learning and daily long Tachanun, and the wonder that only one Jew, an informer, was killed. He compares the first Gulf War, where in Israel the only victim of the Scuds was a man who had been cursed.

title.en: Praying for only one trouble at a time

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk of 'many evils and troubles' that the Chasam Sofer explains, and the Gemara that one may fast and pray for only one trouble at a time. When a city had both plague and hunger, they were told to pray for plenty, since food is given to the living, and so the plague stopped too.

title.en: The bee and the scorpion: contradicting troubles

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Gemara's bee and scorpion: one venom heats and one cools, so a person stung by both cannot be healed, and such troubles will come before Moshiach. The Chasam Sofer applies this to the war: one cannot pray for peace, because war may be the beginning of the geulah, yet the people are suffering.

title.en: Torah is the protection; the war of the mouth

summary.en: The Chasam Sofer answers that 'the shira', the Torah, protects, and the Mashgiach adds tefillah and tzedakah as the Jews' ammunition: the war is decided not by Bush or Saddam but by Jews in batei medrash. He brings Tehillim 149 and the Chazal about Chizkiyahu sleeping calmly on Pesach night while a malach destroyed Sancheirev's camp, showing that the Jews' sword is in their mouth.

title.en: Why Achashverosh made himself king

summary.en: Noting that Bush is pressing for war against the world's opposition, the Mashgiach asks why the Megillah tells that Achashverosh became king by himself, and answers that Hashem appointed him for the salvation of Purim. He compares the Maharal's answer on why the Jews were forced to accept the Torah although they wanted it: what the world depends on is not left to people.

title.en: Involuntary muscles, Bush, and the soldiers of Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach illustrates the Maharal with the heart and lungs, which work without a person's will because life depends on them, and applies the idea to Bush, who became president with fewer votes, so Hashem made him president for a role. He closes that Adar is a month of war against Amalek, fought with Torah, tefillah, tzedakah and resisting the yetzer hara, and that the listeners are the soldiers who will bring victory to Klal Yisrael.

catalogTitle: חכמה - שורש אמונה שהוא למעלה מהשגה. פתי יאמין לכל דבר - לגבי ה' כלנו פתיים. רוב יהודים ימסרו נפשם לה' חוץ אם יש לו קשר לגוי.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains from Tanya chapter 18 that every Jew's emunah comes from chochmah, which is above understanding, so that most Jews will give their lives for Hashem, unless, as the Tzemach Tzedek notes, a connection to the goy has cut them off.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter 18: chochmah is the root of the intellect, a level that cannot be grasped, and the light of the Ein Sof is clothed in it. Since even the lowest Jewish soul contains chochmah, every Jew, even the unlearned, believes in Hashem, for emunah begins where understanding ends. He explains 'a simpleton believes everything' and says that before Hashem all are simpletons, as David HaMelech called himself a beast before Hashem and therefore always with Him. This natural bond, like an animal's devotion to its young, is why even sinners give their lives for kiddush Hashem, as the Toldos story and Jewish history show. Why only 'most'? The Tzemach Tzedek excludes one who eats chametz on Pesach or drinks chalav akum, because these bind a Jew to the goy. The Mashgiach applies this at length to modern culture, media and the internet, and closes with the Torah and sefarim that keep a Jew bound to Hashem.

en: Chochmah is a level above understanding in which the light of the Ein Sof is clothed, and every Jewish soul, even the lowest, contains it.
Emunah means believing what one does not understand, so it comes from chochmah, and therefore even women who do not learn and the unlearned believe in Hashem.
Before Hashem every person is a simpleton, as David HaMelech said he was like a beast before Hashem, and through this he was always with Him.
Even the lowest Jews and sinners, for the most part, give their lives for kiddush Hashem, because a Jew is bound to his Source and cannot tear himself away.
The Tzemach Tzedek notes that one who eats chametz on Pesach or drinks chalav akum is an exception, because these carry a connection to the goy.
The Mashgiach says that today the goy has entered Jewish homes through media and the internet, and this cuts a Jew off from the kedushah of Yisrael.

the Tzemach Tzedek on chametz and chalav akum

title.en: Chochmah above understanding as the root of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter 18 and explains that chochmah is the root of the intellect that cannot be grasped, where the light of the Ein Sof is clothed. Since every Jewish soul contains chochmah, and emunah is belief in what one does not understand, even women and the unlearned believe in Hashem.

title.en: A simpleton believes everything; before Hashem all are simpletons

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the passuk in Mishlei that a simpleton believes everything while the clever one understands, and compares the Jew's inborn emunah to a hen that guards her eggs with no intellect, out of natural love. He concludes that before Hashem all are simpletons, as David HaMelech said he was like a beast before Hashem and therefore always with Him.

title.en: Even sinners give their lives: the story in the Toldos

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that even the lowest Jews and sinners mostly give their lives for kiddush Hashem, because a Jew is bound to Hashem as a child to its parents. He tells the story brought in the Toldos, which chassidim attribute to Adel, the Ba'al Shem Tov's daughter, about a thief who let himself be burned rather than convert.

title.en: Mesirus nefesh in Jewish history, and why only 'most'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings examples from Jewish history: the Crusades, the decrees of Tach v'Tat, and the expulsion from Spain, where whole communities died or left everything rather than convert. He then asks why the Tanya says only 'most', and why some in Spain did convert.

title.en: The Tzemach Tzedek: chametz and chalav akum

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tzemach Tzedek's note that one who eats chametz on Pesach or drinks chalav akum is not among those who give their lives. He explains that chametz is linked to avodah zarah and that chalav akum means having no connection to the goy, which sells a Jew to the klipah called goy; being a goy includes the goy's dress, culture and way of thinking.

title.en: The goy's hatred as a protection; the Ba'al HaTanya and Napoleon

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from Tehillim that Hashem turned the Egyptians' hearts to hate the Jews, and that throughout the galus the goyim's hatred and the ghettos kept Jews from mixing with them. He tells that the Ba'al HaTanya preferred Russian rule to Napoleon, who would give the Jews freedom, because that would be good materially but bad spiritually.

title.en: Infected with the goy in America today

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Jews in America today take on the goy's culture through radio, television, offices, food, literature and news, and contrasts this with Jewish foods that carry kedushah. He brings the pesukim about mixing with the nations and being separated from them, and the special siman in Shulchan Aruch, and returns to chalav akum as the reason a minority will not give their lives.

title.en: Tosfos on wine touched to cause a loss

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a Tosfos in Avodah Zarah that wine a goy touched only to cause the Jew a loss is not yayin nesech, with the proof from a chassid who drank such wine and later gave his life for kiddush Hashem. He explains that by the Tanya's rule, his mesirus nefesh is a sign that the wine was not yayin nesech and the psak was true.

title.en: The goy in the home today, and the remedy of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that earlier non-observant Jews had no connection to the goy, but today the goy has entered everywhere, through books, newspapers, radio and the internet, and shapes the mind as Torah would. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar on lighting Chanukah candles inside, since the public domain has entered the home, and closes that Torah, sefarim and stories of tzaddikim keep a Jew bound to the chochmah of the Ein Sof and to emunah.

catalogTitle: מסירת נפש אפי' בלי דעת כי אמונה למעלה מן דעת. ברית מילה למעלה מן הדעת. ישמעאל וא”י. אהבה מסותרת. “נר ה' נשמת אדם” על פי חסידות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew's emunah is above understanding, which is why even the simplest Jew gives up his life rather than deny Hashem, why bris milah is done on an eight-day-old baby, and how the soul is 'the candle of Hashem'.

abstract.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 18, the Mashgiach explains that every Jew, even the simplest, inherited emunah from the Avos and heard 'Anochi' at Har Sinai, and that this emunah is above daas: before Hashem everyone is a 'peti' who simply believes, and that is the greatest wisdom. Simple Jews who do not think about Hashem's greatness still give up their lives rather than deny Him, not out of fear of Gehinnom or hope for Gan Eden, but because the soul cannot cut itself off from Hashem, just as a person cannot jump off a roof. He then brings the argument of Yishmael and Yitzchak before the Akeidah and asks why milah, the greatest mitzvah, is given to a baby who has no kavanah. His answer: milah is emunah, above daas. He adds that a goy's milah is not milah, that Eretz Yisroel is 'the Jew of geography', and links Chevron to milah and Shechem to periah. Opening chapter 19, he explains 'ner Hashem nishmas adam' through the custom of lighting a Shabbos candle for each child, and begins the image of the flame that always rises.

en: Every Jew, even the simplest, has emunah inherited from Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov and implanted at Har Sinai, and this emunah is above daas.
Before Hashem every person is a 'peti' who simply believes, and believing that way is the greatest wisdom.
Simple Jews give up their lives for emunah not out of reward or punishment but because the soul cannot cut itself off from Hashem.
Milah is given to an eight-day-old baby because milah is emunah, the bond with Avraham Avinu that is above daas.
A goy's milah is not considered milah, since he is entirely orlah, while a Jew has orlah only in one place.
The soul is the 'candle of Hashem', which is why many light another Shabbos candle for each child born.

title.en: Emunah above daas: everyone a 'peti'

summary.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 18, the Mashgiach explains that every Jew inherited emunah from the Avos and heard 'Anochi' at Sinai, and that emunah is above daas. He brings 'peti ya'amin lechol davar' and 'va'ani va'ar velo eida' to show that before Hashem everyone is a simple believer, and that this is the greatest wisdom.

title.en: Why simple Jews give up their lives

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why simple Jews, who do not contemplate Hashem and sin in other areas, still give up their lives rather than deny Him. He answers that it is not fear of Gehinnom or hope of reward, but that the soul cannot cut itself off from Hashem, just as a sane person cannot jump off a roof.

title.en: Yishmael's claim and milah without kavanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi's account of the argument between Yishmael and Yitzchak before the Akeidah. Citing the Shulchan Aruch that milah is the greatest mitzvah, and the question whether mitzvos need kavanah, he contrasts the Ba'al Shem Tov's tefillin with an ordinary person's, and asks why such a mitzvah is given to a baby who cannot have kavanah: was Yishmael right? He answers that milah is above kavanah.

title.en: Milah is emunah; a goy's milah is not milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that milah binds a Jew to Avraham Avinu, the root of emunah, and is therefore done on a baby to show that the bond is above daas. Yishmael's milah is merely a cut: from the Mishnah in Nedarim and the episode of Shechem he shows that a goy, even circumcised, is not called circumcised, because he is entirely orlah while a Jew has orlah in one place only.

title.en: Eretz Yisroel, Chevron and Shechem

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Eretz Yisroel 'the Jew of geography' and explains that milah has two parts, milah and periah: Chevron, where Avraham was circumcised, is the place of milah, and Shechem, linked to Yosef and Yehoshua, is the place of periah, which is why Yaakov's sons cut off its inhabitants. He returns to milah at eight days as emunah above daas, and describes the custom in Eretz Yisroel of saying Shema with closed eyes before a bris.

title.en: Hidden love and a candle for each child

summary.en: Opening Tanya chapter 19, the Mashgiach recalls that every Jew has a hidden love of Hashem that comes out at mesiras nefesh, and introduces 'ner Hashem nishmas adam'. He describes the widespread Ashkenazi custom of lighting two Shabbos candles from the wedding, for zachor and shamor, and adding a candle for each child, because each child is another soul, another light.

title.en: The soul as a flame that rises

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'ner Hashem nishmas adam' as the Tanya does: the soul is like the light of a candle, which constantly flickers upward. He notes that fire has no solidity, yet unlike water on a slope it does not fall but rises, and leaves the question of why for the next shiur.

catalogTitle: נשמות ישראל כמו נר לאבוקה לגבי ה' הם בטלים אצלו. מכת חושך. יין של פורים. ביטול הוא מהות הקדושה וסטרא אחרא להיפוך. לחיים יא”צ הר”ר זישא.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 19, the Mashgiach explains that the soul's longing to be nullified in Hashem like a candle in a torch comes from chochmah, the root of all kedushah, which is bittul, while the sitra achra is the opposite: self-importance even in giving.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach learns Tanya chapter 19: like a candle flame drawn into a great torch even though it will be extinguished, every level of the soul longs to return to its Root, Hashem, the true Father who gives it every breath. This longing is beyond reason because it stems from chochmah, which cannot be grasped. He ties chochmah to the plague of darkness: there is a darkness of light too great to absorb, which is why 'borei choshech' is a higher word than 'yotzer ohr'. Purim brings down such a hidden light of chochmah, so its wine is different, just as wool becomes tzitzis. The Tanya then says all kedushah is bittul. The Mashgiach explains true humility through Moshe Rabbeinu, signatures of 'hakatan', receiving from a Rebbe, and the Chernobyl story of the son who took 'nothing'. The sitra achra is the reverse: even its kindness, like a merchant's, seeks a return. He closes with a l'chaim for the yahrzeit of Rebbe Reb Zusha.

en: Like a candle drawn into a torch, every level of the soul longs to return to Hashem, its Root, even though it would be completely nullified there.
This longing is above reason because it comes from the chochmah of the soul, which is beyond understanding.
The plague of darkness corresponds to chochmah: a light so great that it appears as darkness, and Purim brings down a hidden light of this kind.
The rule of kedushah is bittul: whatever is holy is nullified before Hashem, and this is the true meaning of humility.
The sitra achra is the opposite: even when its people give, they give for themselves and want something back.

title.en: A candle drawn into the torch

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter 19: like a candle flame drawn into a torch, every level of the soul longs to return to Hashem, the true Father, even at the cost of being nullified. He explains that this nature is above reason because it stems from the chochmah of the soul.

title.en: The plague of darkness and chochmah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the plague of darkness corresponds to chochmah: there is a darkness that is light too intense to absorb, which is why the blessing says 'borei choshech', a higher word than 'yotzer ohr'. Purim brings down such a hidden light of chochmah all day, which is why it is tied to Esther and to concealment.

title.en: Why Purim wine is different

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks whether Purim wine is not the same wine as all year, and answers with meshalim: an esrog, wool made into tzitzis and leather made into tefillin straps become different things once holy names rest on them. Wine on an ordinary day is shown in a bad light, Kiddush and Pesach wine carry their own holy names, and Purim wine is 'yayin hameshumar', equal in gematria to Esther.

title.en: Kedushah is bittul: true humility

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's rule that all kedushah is drawn from chochmah, which is nullified before the Ein Sof. He explains that humility is not walking with a lowered head, which is really a form of pride, but being batel to Hashem like Moshe Rabbeinu, who was a king; he illustrates with the capital 'I' in English, the signature 'hakatan' of gedolim, and the small aleph of Vayikra.

title.en: Bittul before Hashem, a Rebbe and a friend

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one who knows Shas and boasts of it has pride, and compares the boaster to a fly claiming to be bigger than another fly beside the Empire State Building. A Yid is batel to Hashem, to his friend and to his Rebbe; one can receive from a Rebbe only when one feels smaller, like a cup held below the bottle's spout.

title.en: Koach mah and the son who took nothing

summary.en: The Mashgiach laments that today much is imitation and bittul is missing. Returning to the Tanya, he explains that chochmah is 'koach mah', from Moshe Rabbeinu's 'venachnu mah', the highest humility compared with Avraham's 'afar va'efer' and Dovid's 'tola'as'. He tells of Reb Mordechai of Chernobyl's sons, each of whom took one of his father's middos, while the youngest took his 'nothing'.

title.en: The sitra achra: giving in order to get

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that the sitra achra is the opposite of bittul: the nations act for themselves even in charity, for honor and a monument. He maps the seven nations of Eretz Yisroel against the seven middos, with Canaan as chesed, and explains from Rashi why a merchant is called a 'Canaani' and why 'socher' means going around in a circle: the grocer gives in order to get back. The chesed of kedushah gives without wanting anything back.

title.en: L'chaim for Rebbe Reb Zusha's yahrzeit

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that it is the yahrzeit of Rebbe Reb Zusha and makes a l'chaim, with an exchange about the drink and about bishul. He tells how Rebbe Reb Zusha's fear of Heaven was so great that a word of kabbalah alone would overwhelm him, and mentions the Chernobyl custom of saying Parshas Haman on the Tuesday of Beshalach.

catalogTitle: הספד: על האדמו”ר מסאטמאר זצ”ל

oneLiner.en: In a hesped for the Satmar Rebbe, the Mashgiach describes his tireless avodas Hashem and explains that his fierce battle was for the pure geulah of Moshiach as the Rambam defines it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that although the sun and the earth are unchanged, the world is different after the passing of the Satmar Rebbe, whose voice of Torah and tefillah has been silenced. As a neighbor he would look into the Rebbe's lit windows late at night and before dawn and see him immersed in avodas Hashem; except for Shabbos he never went to bed. He recalls that Rav Reuven Grozovsky consulted him and said the whole Torah was open to him, and that crowds waited for hours for his brachah. Turning to the huge funeral, he explains that the Rebbe was controversial because he feared that Jews would mistake the founding of the state for the geulah. He fought like a lion for the true geulah described by the Rambam, and even an opponent admitted that the Rebbe kept them in check.

en: After the Satmar Rebbe's passing the world is a different world, because the voice of a tzaddik's Torah and tefillah has been silenced.
The Mashgiach saw from his windows that the Rebbe was immersed in avodas Hashem at all hours and, except on Shabbos, never went to bed.
The Rebbe opposed the state because he feared people would mistake its founding for the geulah and treat its leader as Moshiach.
The geulah he awaited was the pure one the Rambam describes, led by a king from the house of David who brings the whole world to serve Hashem together.
Because of his constant fight, Jews still hold on to the belief in the coming of Moshiach as one of the principles of faith.

candidateTopics: belief in the coming of Moshiach

title.en: A neighbor's memories of the Satmar Rebbe

summary.en: The Mashgiach laments that the world is different now that the Satmar Rebbe's voice is silenced, and recalls seeing him through his lit windows at night immersed in avodas Hashem. He tells of Rav Reuven Grozovsky's admiration for him and of the crowds who waited hours for his brachah.

title.en: His fight for the true geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the huge funeral and explains that the Rebbe was controversial because he feared the state would be mistaken for the geulah. He lays out the Rambam's description of Moshiach as the geulah the Rebbe awaited, cites an opponent's admission that the Rebbe kept them in check, and concludes that thanks to him Jews still believe in Moshiach.

catalogTitle: יש גוי בתוך יהודי - ועל זה צריך לעשות תשובה. אצל רשעים הנפש אלקות בגלות והיא אנוס לעשות עבירה - זה גלות השכינה. בעצם חכמה אין פגם אבל בהתפשטות החכמה יש פגם וזה פוגם בחכמה ממש.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 19, the Mashgiach explains that a sinning Jew drags his G-dly soul into exile, yet the very root of its chochmah stays untouched and wakes up in a test of emunah, which is why even a sinner gives his life for kiddush Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the reading of the sefarim that 'the stranger in your midst' of the tochachah is the goy inside every Jew, and cites a student of the Ba'al Shem Tov that one must do teshuvah for it before Shabbos; he tells of a Breslover ger who would roar at night to cut the goy out of himself. Following Tanya chapter 19, he explains that the sinner submits to the yetzer hara and forces his G-dly soul into exile, which is galus haShechinah, like a captured prince forced to fight his own father. The hidden love inherited from Avraham Avinu is only covered. He then resolves a contradiction: the essence of chochmah is never touched by sin, but its spreading into the heart is, and that essence sleeps until a test of emunah wakes it. He illustrates this with a story of the Czar and a Jewish soldier, and, on the yahrzeit of the Rayatz, with stories of his mesiras nefesh and his holiness.

en: The Mashgiach explains that 'the stranger in your midst' refers to the aspect of a goy inside a Jew, and that one must do teshuvah for it before entering Shabbos.
When a Jew sins, even an otherwise upright Jew, his G-dly soul is in exile and is forced to take part in the sin; this is galus haShechinah.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem, an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, which in a sinner is covered by a garment of klipah but never lost.
The essence of chochmah in the soul is not blemished by sin; only its spreading into the heart and the whole person is.
In ordinary sins the chochmah sleeps, but a test of emunah reaches it and wakes it, so even the lowest Jew gives his life rather than deny Hashem.

candidateTopics: hidden love inherited from Avraham Avinu

title.en: The goy within every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the reading of the sefarim that 'the stranger in your midst' is the goy inside a Jew, and a student of the Ba'al Shem Tov who said one must do teshuvah for it before Shabbos. He tells of a ger among the Breslover chassidim who would roar at night to cut the goy out of himself.

title.en: The G-dly soul in exile: galus haShechinah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the sinner submits to the yetzer hara in the left side of the heart rather than to his G-dly soul, yet before the test of emunah of the first two commandments he gives his life. He reads the Tanya that the sinner's G-dly soul is in exile and is forced into the sin, which is galus haShechinah, and stresses this applies to any Jew when he sins.

title.en: The captive prince and the hidden love

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives the mashal of a prince captured by his father's enemies and forced to fight against his father, and explains the Tanya's 'hidden love' through the passuk in Mishlei: an inheritance from Avraham Avinu that in a sinner is covered by klipah. He then reads that a spirit of folly enters through this covering, and that the exile reaches only the spreading of chochmah.

title.en: Essence of chochmah versus its spreading

summary.en: The Mashgiach raises a contradiction: earlier the Tanya said sin does not reach the chochmah, yet here the sinner drags it into exile. He answers that the essence of chochmah, the emunah, cannot be touched, but its spreading into the heart and the whole body, like the sun's rays, is blemished; the root stays in the brain.

title.en: The sleeping chochmah wakes at a test of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that during sin the chochmah in the brain sleeps, but a test of emunah, which is above reason, wakes it, so even the worst sinner refuses to separate from Hashem. He contrasts the tzaddik who rules his heart with the rasha ruled by it, and brings pesukim that before Hashem all the klipos melt away.

title.en: The Czar and the Jewish soldier

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story known among Russian chassidim: a Czar in disguise drinks with a Jewish soldier who pawns his sword for drink, escapes the Czar's trap with a wooden sword, and rises to general. When ordered to convert, the soldier, who had committed every sin, leaps from a bridge into the water, and the Czar remarks that a Jew gives his life when it comes to mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The Rayatz's mesiras nefesh in Soviet Russia

summary.en: Noting the yahrzeit of the Lubavitcher Rebbe Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak, the Mashgiach tells how he kept up hidden chadarim, yeshivos, davening and mikva'os under the Communists, was arrested, and answered the commissar's revolver that he has one G-d and two worlds. He adds the Machnovker Rebbe's words that only Breslover and Lubavitcher chassidim came to him in Russia, and that hundreds of Lubavitcher chassidim were killed for their mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim's granddaughter

summary.en: The Mashgiach retells what Rabbi Shimshon Pincus heard from a granddaughter of the Chofetz Chaim: as a young woman leaving Yiddishkeit she boasted to her grandfather of telephones, radio and bombs, and he foretold flights across the Atlantic, flight to the moon and a bomb that destroys a whole city, yet she stayed as she was. He contrasts this with the Yiddishkeit the Rayatz and his chassidim kept alive in Russia through mesiras nefesh.

title.en: Stories of the young Rayatz

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the young Rayatz, working as secretary for a wealthy chassid, sensed which of a dealer's vessels truly belonged to a tzaddik, lifting each twice after doing teshuvah in case a sin dulled his sense. He then tells how Reb Peretz Chaim, bending down to pick up a coin the Rebbe's son had dropped while juggling by a window, escaped a Communist's bullet, and the shiur ends with l'chaim.

catalogTitle: כל עבירה היא ע”ז ממש והעובר הוא יותר גרוע מהסטרא אחרא ממש. הסטרא אחרא נהנה מבחינת אחוריים. אם חוטא' יתוש קדמך. תרץ למה אין כל עבירה דוחה פיקוח נפש אם כל עבירה היא ע”ז ממש.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 24, the Mashgiach explains that every sin, even a small one, is truly avodah zarah, that the sinner is lower than the sitra achra itself and even than a gnat, and why pikuach nefesh nevertheless overrides most sins.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach announces he will now learn faster, recalls chapter 23 (anochi as the root of all mitzvos, lo yihyeh of all sins), and opens chapter 24: just as Torah and mitzvos unite a Jew with Hashem, a sin unites him with the sitra achra. Every sin is avodah zarah because the sinner makes himself a yesh who will not be batel to Hashem's will, like chametz that rises against humble matzah. He uses the very G-dly soul that animates him to power the sin, lending the sitra achra a body. The sitra achra still knows its Master and does His will; the sinner does not. It lives only from the outermost 'back' of holiness, the dregs that cannot be refined. A person sins only through a spirit of folly that hides the truth from his chochmah. Like the gnat that only takes and never gives, the sinner is lower than all creatures, and animals rule a man only when he loses his tzelem Elokim, with stories of tzaddikim and beasts. Finally the Mashgiach asks why pikuach nefesh overrides ordinary sins and answers from the Gemara and as a gezeiras hakasuv.

en: Every sin, even a rabbinic one, is truly avodah zarah, because the sinner detaches himself from bittul to Hashem and binds himself to the sitra achra.
A sin is a yesh, a self that will not be batel to Hashem's will, and the yesh itself is avodah zarah, as chametz rises while matzah stays low.
When sinning, a Jew harnesses his G-dly soul, which gives his body life, to the sitra achra, and lends it a body with which to sin.
The sitra achra itself recognizes its Master and carries out His will, so a person who sins is worse than it.
A person sins only because a spirit of folly covers his chochmah; were it uncovered, he would give his life rather than sin, as he would for avodah zarah.
Pikuach nefesh overrides other sins not because they are lighter than avodah zarah but because of the Gemara's reasoning and a decree of the Torah.

title.en: Faster pace; review of chapter 23

summary.en: The Mashgiach says he will now learn faster, just to know what the text says, so as to reach the later chapters. He recalls chapter 23: anochi is the root of all mitzvos and lo yihyeh of all sins, so every sin is avodah zarah, and asks why a person who would give his life rather than worship idols does not make the same calculation for every sin.

title.en: A sin as union with the sitra achra

summary.en: Opening chapter 24, the Mashgiach explains that just as Torah study unites a person with Hashem, a sin unites him with the sitra achra. The sinner is a yesh who will not be batel, and a yesh is avodah zarah; he illustrates with chametz, which rises, against matzah, which stays low, and with haughtiness.

title.en: The G-dly soul harnessed to the sin

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that through thought, speech and action of a sin the soul itself is united with avodah zarah: the G-dly soul that animates the body is made into a horse pulling the wagon of the sin, and the sinner lends the sitra achra a body. He adds that the sitra achra knows its Master and does His will, so the sinner is worse than it.

title.en: The sitra achra lives from the 'back'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that even idol-worshippers call Hashem the G-d of gods and believe He handed the world to lesser powers; their sin is that they consider themselves a yesh. Everything must draw some life from holiness, and the sitra achra draws only from the 'back', the part that cannot be refined, like the waste of food; the sinner, who goes against Hashem's will, is worse.

title.en: Dregs of this world and the spirit of folly

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the evil of this material world is the dregs of the kelipos, like the sediment of spoiled wine, which is why the wicked are strong here. He brings the Gemara that a person sins only when a spirit of folly enters him, and explains why the woman of the parsha of sotah would give her life rather than bow to an idol yet commits a sin: the folly covers her chochmah, which is roused only by real avodah zarah.

title.en: Even the gnat preceded you

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that a gnat was created before man and explains it: every creature both receives from the world and gives to it, like the bee, but the gnat only sucks blood and gives nothing, the very mark of the sitra achra. Yet a sinner, who goes against Hashem's will, is lower still; he tells of a tzaddik who would not kill any creature except a mosquito.

title.en: Beasts and the tzelem Elokim: stories

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Chazal that a wild beast rules over a man only when he looks to it like an animal, having lost his tzelem Elokim. He tells how lions bowed before the Divrei Chaim, how a pack of wolves left a family of the Komarna Rebbe's descendants unharmed, and of a gadol who saw a leader without a tzelem Elokim; and he mentions Daniel among the lions.

title.en: Why pikuach nefesh overrides other sins

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks: if every sin is avodah zarah, why does pikuach nefesh override all sins but avodah zarah? He answers with the Gemara's reasoning, desecrate one Shabbos so he can keep many, and that it is a gezeiras hakasuv, not because Shabbos is lighter; he shows from the law of shechitah that a mumar for Shabbos is like an idolater. He closes with a word about the coming week.

catalogTitle: אין אדם חוטא אלא אם נכנס בו רוח שטות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew sins only because a spirit of folly makes him forget that every sin cuts him off from Hashem just as idolatry does, and that the same readiness for mesirus nefesh he would show against idolatry can carry him through every daily battle with the yetzer hara.

abstract.en: Learning Tanya chapter 25, the Mashgiach recalls that even the simplest Jews gave their lives rather than worship idols in the persecutions of Europe, and teaches that every sin is a branch of idolatry, since it too separates a person from Hashem. A Jew sins only because a spirit of folly, as the Gemara says, makes him forget this; his hidden love for Hashem is always there. Even the plan to sin and then repent does not help, since the bond with Hashem is above time and even one moment of separation counts. The Mashgiach applies the reckoning to the daily war: getting up to daven, learning with clarity and full strength, davening with kavanah, giving tzedakah. He adds that a mitzvah creates an eternal union, warns about wasted time, and cautions that today's weaker generations must also guard their health. He closes with Rashi's reading that going against one's will is itself mesirus nefesh, and explains why the generation in the desert also needed the mitzvah of mesirus nefesh.

en: Every sin, even a light one, is a branch of idolatry, because it too separates a Jew from Hashem.
A Jew sins only because a spirit of folly enters him and he forgets that the sin cuts him off from Hashem; his hidden love stays intact.
The bond with Hashem is above time, so even a single moment of separation is real separation, and the plan to sin and repent later changes nothing.
The same reckoning of mesirus nefesh should be used against the yetzer hara in getting up to daven, learning Torah with clarity and full strength, davening with kavanah and giving tzedakah.
A mitzvah or Torah learning creates a union with Hashem that is eternal, while time spent on idle things loses that union.
Today's generations are weaker than in the Ba'al HaTanya's time, so a person must also look after his health, as long as most of the day is given to Torah and avodah.
Going against one's own will is itself a form of mesirus nefesh, and the readiness to give one's life should be applied to all the mitzvos.

candidateTopics: every sin as a branch of idolatry

title.en: Every Jew gives his life against idolatry

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that in the decrees and persecutions of Europe hundreds of thousands of simple Jews gave their lives rather than convert, and explains that every sin, even a light one, is a branch of idolatry. He says a person must sit and think about this again and again until it becomes part of his own knowledge.

title.en: The spirit of folly and the plan to repent later

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that a person sins only when a spirit of folly enters him: he forgets that the sin separates him from Hashem, while his hidden love, which includes fear, remains. He then shows that even one who plans to repent afterwards would still give his life rather than bow to an idol even for a moment, because the bond with Hashem is above time.

title.en: Using the reckoning in daily avodah

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the reckoning to the yetzer hara's daily tricks: the laziness to get up and daven in the morning, learning without clarity and full strength, davening without kavanah, and holding back from giving tzedakah. Even for one minute, he says, a Jew would give his life rather than be cut off, so he can overcome these smaller tests.

title.en: The eternal union of a mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a mitzvah done with all one's strength makes a union with Hashem that lasts forever, since above everything is eternal and the Torah never changes. Time wasted on idle talk and things that have nothing to do with Torah or avodah loses that union, and one must then ask Hashem's forgiveness.

title.en: Weaker generations and guarding health

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Ba'al HaTanya demanded unbroken Torah and avodah of people stronger than today's, and that those who strain too much break down. A person must rest, eat properly and exercise for his health, which is not bittul Torah, as long as most of the day is given to Torah and avodah and he does not indulge in foolishness.

title.en: Selach lanu and the meaning of nafsheichem

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Chazal instituted the brachah of Selach lanu three times a day, and answers that it is for bittul Torah, which the daily tamid offering used to atone for and which the tefillos now replace. He then brings Rashi that nefesh means will, so that anyone who acts against his will has a measure of mesirus nefesh.

title.en: Mesirus nefesh in Shema and in the desert

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when saying Shema one must have in mind readiness for mesirus nefesh at the word echad and at bechol nafshecha. He asks why the generation in the desert, whom Hashem promised the nations would fear, needed the mitzvah of mesirus nefesh, and answers that it let them make the reckoning for every mitzvah and every small sin.

catalogTitle: נשים: Marriage - a Union of קדושה and נצחיות

oneLiner.en: From Parshas Chayei Sarah the Mashgiach shows that a Jewish marriage is a union of kedushah and eternity, and that a Jewish home, its clothing and its toil for chesed are an extension of the Beis HaMikdash.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by explaining why he speaks in English, with the Chazon Ish's parable that the battlefront moves, and the teaching that the Torah was explained in seventy languages. He then asks why a sedra that opens with Sarah's passing is called Chayei Sarah, and why the word for Avraham's weeping has a small kaf. His answer: a Jewish shidduch is decreed before birth, a reunion of souls, and death does not end it. Avraham prepared the Me'aras HaMachpelah as a home where the couple stays united, so Sarah remains alive as his wife. In a personal note he thanks the community for the home they built him, whose soul is the love put into it, like the Beis HaMikdash. Through Tehillim 128 and Rav Hirsch he teaches that every Jewish home is an extension of Tziyon, with a dress code like the Kohanim. He ends with Rivka's chesed and two stories showing that toil for chesed redeems a person from other toil.

en: A Jewish shidduch is decreed before birth; it is a reunion of souls that were already united.
A Jewish marriage is netzach: death separates bodies but not souls, and the couple remains united.
The sedra is called Chayei Sarah because Sarah remains alive as Avraham's wife; her levayah is the introduction to the shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka.
What counts in a building, like the Beis HaMikdash, is its inner soul: the love with which it was built.
Every Jewish home, wherever it is, can be an extension of Tziyon, with its family as Kohanim and its meals bearing the holiness of korbanos.
The clothing and jewelry of a Jewish man and woman, like the Kohanim's garments, must radiate Torah.
Each person is allotted a measure of toil; toil spent on chesed redeems him from other toil.

candidateTopics: the jewish home as an extension of the Beis HaMikdash
tznius and the garments of the Kohanim
teaching in the language children understand

title.en: Why the Mashgiach speaks in English

summary.en: Asked to speak in English, the Mashgiach explains that Yiddish once united Jews but is now spoken only in isolated communities. He tells how the Chazon Ish answered a complaint about a cheder taught in Ivrit with a parable of an old soldier at a battlefront that has moved, and brings the teaching that the Torah was explained in seventy languages: what matters is that it be understood.

title.en: Chayei Sarah: mourning or wedding?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a sedra that opens with Sarah's passing is called Chayei Sarah, and why the kaf of Avraham's weeping is small; he finds the Ba'al HaTurim's answer difficult. Noting that the sedra moves straight from the levayah to the shidduch of Yitzchak and Rivka, he asks whether one should mourn or rejoice with it, and answers that the whole sedra is really a wedding, since a shidduch is decreed before birth and is a reunion of souls.

title.en: A marriage that death does not end

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jewish marriage is netzach: the couple is united before birth and after death. Avraham at once prepared the Me'aras HaMachpelah, where each couple lies side by side, as a home where he and Sarah remain united; this explains the small kaf, and why the sedra is called Chayei Sarah. He ties this to kiddushin, to the kesubah's commitment in life and beyond, and calls Sarah's levayah the introduction to the first shidduch in the Torah: kedushah and eternity.

title.en: A personal note: a home with a soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Shir HaShirim about the apiryon of Shlomo HaMelech and the Alshich's explanation that the gold and silver of the Beis HaMikdash were only its body, while its soul was the flaming love with which it was built. He then thanks the men and boys of Emunas Yisroel, through their wives, for the residence they prepared for him and his wife with so much warmth, and notes that it opens onto the beis medrash.

title.en: Every home an extension of Tziyon

summary.en: Through Tehillim 128 the Mashgiach visits the home of the one who fears Hashem and asks where Tziyon comes in. He reads Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch: such a person sees his home as a branch of the sphere whose center is Yerushalayim. Every home can therefore be an extension of Tziyon, its family Kohanim, and like the Kohanim it has a dress code set by the Torah.

title.en: Rivka's jewelry and her test of chesed

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that the bracelets Eliezer gave Rivka, like her home, had a soul: Torah and the Luchos, which the jewelry radiated. Using what he read about how much water a camel stores, he calculates that watering ten camels meant drawing about four hundred gallons: the demanding test of chesed that showed she was fit for the house of Avraham.

title.en: Toil for chesed redeems other toil

summary.en: Addressing the women of Emunas Yisroel gathered to help kallahs set up their homes, the Mashgiach says such work demands toil, and that each year's toil is decreed on Rosh Hashanah. He tells of Rav Shlomke of Zvhil and the lost gold watch, brings the Gemara that man is born to toil, and tells of a chassid of Rav Aharon of Karlin who suffered in the street what he would not suffer at home. Toil for hachnasas kallah redeems a person from other toil, and he closes with blessings.

catalogTitle: היצר מנצח כשאדם בעצבות' קשר עצבות לעצלות. בכל עצב יהיה מותר. עצה להיות בשמחה אפ' כשבאות צרות.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 26, the Mashgiach explains why sadness lets the yetzer hara win, how a set time of broken-heartedness leads to a greater joy, and why sadness that comes in the middle of business or avodah is a trick of the yetzer.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach learns the opening of Tanya chapter 26: just as a sluggish wrestler loses even to a weaker opponent, a person in sadness cannot defeat the yetzer, because sadness and laziness both come from the element of earth. One must be joyful, free of worry about the future and of dissatisfaction with the present. He then explains the verse 'in every sadness there is an advantage': a broken heart at a set time, as in the Arizal's order of Tikkun Chatzos followed by Tehillim 51, leads to a joy greater than before, like light after darkness. Along the way he discusses the four tefillos and four Shabbos meals, staying awake on leil shishi and Shavuos night, and the hidden chassadim that come clothed in suffering. He closes with the Tanya's warning that sadness during business or davening is a ploy of the yetzer, which leads to cravings.

en: Like a sluggish wrestler who loses to a weaker opponent, a person in sadness and heaviness cannot overcome the yetzer hara.
Sadness and laziness come from the same element of earth; a sad person lacks the joy of life and moves slowly, while zerizus comes from joy.
'In every sadness there is an advantage': the joy that comes after a true broken heart at a set time is greater, like light that comes after darkness.
Regret over one's avodah belongs only at a fixed time, such as after Tikkun Chatzos or at Krias Shema before sleep, not all day.
Suffering that comes from the hidden world is a greater kindness, and great tzaddikim rejoiced in suffering because it bound them to Hashem.
Sadness about one's spiritual standing that falls on a person in the middle of business or davening comes from the yetzer hara, which uses it to lead him to cravings.

candidateTopics: in every sadness there is an advantage
