title.en: Sadness and laziness lose the battle

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter 26 and its mashal of two wrestlers, adding the example of the lion and the ox. He explains that sadness and laziness both come from the element of earth, so a depressed person moves slowly and cannot defeat the yetzer.

title.en: Joy, zerizus and waking up early

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's call to be free of worry and sadness, distinguishing worry about the future from dissatisfaction with the present. He shows that people who wake up late are escaping life, while on a day they expect something good they rise early, as a Jew who looks forward to serving Hashem does.

title.en: In every sadness there is an advantage

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the verse 'in every sadness there is an advantage' and explains with the Tanya that the advantage is the joy that follows true regret over one's avodah. A broken heart breaks the sitra achra and the wall between a person and Hashem, as the verse 'the offerings of G-d are a broken spirit' teaches.

title.en: A set time for sadness: Tikkun Chatzos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sadness may enter only at an appointed time, for a few minutes. He shows this in the Arizal's order to say Tehillim 51, Dovid HaMelech's chapter of teshuvah, after Tikkun Chatzos, where one mourns the destruction of his own inner Beis HaMikdash and then learns in joy.

title.en: Four tefillos, four meals, and leil shishi

summary.en: The Mashgiach digresses to the four tefillos: Shacharis and Mincha are obligations, Maariv was a choice that Jews accepted like a vow, and Dovid HaMelech's midnight tefillah remained for tzaddikim. He parallels them to the four Shabbos meals, and criticizes staying up on Thursday night only to sleep through Shabbos.

title.en: Shavuos night and serving with sense

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that staying awake on Shavuos night is meant to prepare for the morning, so one who will doze through davening and Kerias HaTorah gains nothing, like a chasan who arranged everything and then went to sleep at the chuppah. Since the generations have weakened, one must serve Hashem with sense, and on Shabbos rise early, learn and daven with strength.

title.en: Light after darkness; sorrows of this world

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains with 'as light excels over darkness' that joy after sadness is greater, and brings the Arizal's reading of 'because you did not serve Hashem with joy'. He lists other set times for a reckoning, then turns to sadness over children, health and livelihood, which the Tanya rejects, since one blesses Hashem for bad as for good.

title.en: Hidden chassadim clothed in suffering

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that rejoicing in suffering is a high level reached through years of work. The first two letters of Hashem's name stand for the hidden worlds, whose greater chassadim come down covered in suffering, as he shows in the word 'mitzvah', and he brings 'fortunate is the man whom Hashem chastises' and Chazal on those who rejoice in suffering.

title.en: Tzaddikim who rejoiced in suffering

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of tzaddikim who rejoiced in suffering, including a Rav named Eliyahu who put his hand into fire, because closeness to Hashem is better than life. He explains that the hidden chassadim will one day be revealed like the sun leaving its sheath, and that in worldly troubles one should bind himself to Hashem.

title.en: Sadness in business and avodah is the yetzer

summary.en: The Mashgiach says simpler people should meet worldly troubles with bitachon. He then brings the Tanya that even sadness over spiritual matters, when it comes during business or davening, is a trick of the yetzer that leads to cravings, as seen in people who overeat, and that true bitterness belongs only at a fixed time such as chatzos or Krias Shema before sleep.

catalogTitle: חילוק בין עצבות ומרירות. כשמחשבות רעות באות - אז יש אפשרות לקיים מצוות ולא תתורו. שני מטעמים שהשכינה נהנות מהם. לחיים יא”צ.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 27, the Mashgiach explains that a bad thought pushed away is not a reason for sadness but a chance to fulfill 'velo sasuru', and that the beinoni's struggle with his yetzer gives Hashem a nachas ruach of its own.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by distinguishing atzvus (dejection that makes a person withdraw and sleep) from merirus (bitterness that drives him to act), and two sources of atzvus: sins and worldly troubles. Turning to Tanya chapter 27, he explains that a person troubled by bad thoughts should not see them as a sign of distance from Hashem: pushing them out fulfills the mitzvah of 'velo sasuru', which speaks to beinonim, not tzaddikim. With the Bnei Yissaschar he shows that the sin lies only in letting the thought stay. In a long digression he explains that the Torah speaks to every Jew on his level, with examples of pride, anger, 'vachai bahem' and Korach. He then brings the Zohar on the nachas ruach when the sitra achra is subdued, the two kinds of 'matamim', 'leyom ra'ah', iskafya in permitted things such as delaying a meal, and 'kadesh atzmecha'. He closes with a lechayim for the yahrzeit of Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz and two stories about him.

en: Atzvus is dejection that makes a person withdraw from life, while merirus is bitterness that pushes him to act; the Mashgiach says atzvus must be avoided.
A bad thought that enters a person's mind is no sign of distance from Hashem; pushing it out fulfills the mitzvah of 'velo sasuru', and he should rejoice in it.
The sin is not that the thought came, but letting it stay and following it; the mitzvah is to drive it out.
When a beinoni subdues the sitra achra, Hashem has a great nachas ruach, a different kind from the nachas of tzaddikim who nullify it entirely.
Iskafya applies even in permitted things, such as holding back from eating for a while when one is hungry, and a little sanctification below brings great kedushah from above.

title.en: Atzvus versus merirus

summary.en: The Mashgiach defines atzvus as dejection that makes a person sleep and avoid reality, and merirus as bitterness that drives him to act. He distinguishes atzvus over sins from atzvus over worldly troubles such as business, children and health.

title.en: Bad thoughts as a chance for a mitzvah

summary.en: Reading Tanya chapter 27, the Mashgiach explains that a person who is pained by bad thoughts, thinking they show he is far from Hashem, is mistaken: when he pushes them away he fulfills 'velo sasuru acharei levavchem'. He asks whether one should then want such thoughts, and begins to answer that the pasuk does not speak to tzaddikim.

title.en: The beinoni's mitzvah of driving thoughts out

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'velo sasuru' speaks to beinonim, each with his own nisyonos, and brings Chazal that one who refrains from a sin that came his way is rewarded as for a mitzvah. With the Bnei Yissaschar he shows the sin is only in keeping the thought, calls distress over such thoughts a form of gasus haruach, and says pushing them out is a person's avodah.

title.en: The Torah speaks to each Jew on his level

summary.en: Pausing to explain the Tanya's claim that the pasuk does not speak to tzaddikim, the Mashgiach says every word of the Torah concerns every Jew: pshat binds everyone, while great tzaddikim keep the Torah on deeper levels. He illustrates with pride and anger, 'vachai bahem', Korach's subtle jealousy, and Moshe's sin at Mei Merivah.

title.en: Subduing the sitra achra raises Hashem's glory

summary.en: Back to the Tanya, the Mashgiach gives the example of a person in the street who remembers not to look and does not look: his mitzvah rises above and the sitra achra is knocked down. He brings the Zohar on the great nachas ruach when the sitra achra is subdued, and says a person plagued all his life by such thoughts should not be broken, since this may be why his soul came down.

title.en: Why a beinoni is created, and two kinds of nachas

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the question from Tanya chapter 1 on free choice and explains the answer here: a beinoni is created to fight the sitra achra without nullifying it, and his war brings a second kind of nachas ruach beside that of tzaddikim. He connects this to the plural 'matamim' of Yitzchak and Rivkah.

title.en: Sweet and sharp delicacies; iskafya in permitted things

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the two kinds of nachas ruach to sweet dishes and sharp ones like horseradish made tasty with fish. He reads 'vegam rasha leyom ra'ah' as making day out of the bad, and explains that iskafya applies even in permitted things, such as delaying a meal for a while when one is hungry.

title.en: A little sanctity below, much from above

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara on the hours when people and talmidei chachamim eat, explaining that the talmid chacham waited to subdue his yetzer, and extends this to holding back from idle talk. He explains that even a little iskafya draws great kedushah from above, citing 'adam mekadesh atzmo me'at' and 'kadesh atzmecha bemutar lach', and the Tanya that true kedushah comes only through subduing the sitra achra.

title.en: Lechayim for the Ropshitzer's yahrzeit

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls for a lechayim for the yahrzeit of Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz and tells of him: a man who wore sackcloth with his shirt open so it would be seen, of whom the Ropshitzer said the Satan had caught him in the sack, and the Ropshitzer's own last words about the yetzer hara.

catalogTitle: תפילה היא מלחמה גדולה' זוכים לבא בהיכלות התיבות ע”י שמחה ויגיעה. מלחמת הגוף והנשמה כל ימי חייו. טעם שהמחשבות רעות בואת דוקא כשעוסקים בעבודת ה'. כלל גדול בעבודת ה' - “אין עוד מלבדו”. לחיים יא”צ ר' שלומקע זווילער זצוקללה”ה.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 28, the Mashgiach explains that foreign thoughts during davening are part of the lifelong war between the two souls, and that the way to win is to dismiss them as nothing, with joy and the great rule 'ein od milvado'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 28 by calling davening a great war: each word of tefillah is a heichal (chamber) above, and a foreign thought is a sign that one is being kept out of it, much as the cherubim guarded Gan Eden. The Tanya says not to sink into sadness but to push in. He explains that a thought is a complete spiritual entity, so a tzaddik can elevate foreign thoughts that come to him from others, but a person whose thoughts are his own must not try. Rather he should strengthen himself with joy, knowing the thought comes from the klipah fighting the G-dly soul; it attacks precisely when one strengthens himself in avodah. Because a person has two souls, such thoughts do not show that his davening is worthless. The answer is bittul: treating them as nothing, by the great rule 'ein od milvado'. He closes with the yahrzeit of Reb Shlomke of Zvil and stories about him.

en: Each word of davening is a heichal above; a foreign thought during tefillah means one is being held back from entering it.
Elevating foreign thoughts is only for tzaddikim, whose foreign thoughts come from others; a person whose thoughts are his own must not engage with them.
One must not fall into sadness over such thoughts, but strengthen himself all the more in davening with joy.
The foreign thought comes from the klipah fighting the G-dly soul in the beinoni, a lifelong war in which each side strengthens itself when the other does.
Because a person has two souls, foreign thoughts in davening are not a sign that his davening is worthless.
The way to deal with them is bittul: to treat them as nothing, by the great rule 'ein od milvado', that besides Hashem everything is nothing.

title.en: Davening as a war for the heichalos

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 28 and explains that each word of davening is a heichal; angels keep a person out with foreign thoughts, like the cherubim at Gan Eden. The Tanya says not to be sad but to push one's way in, as chassidim used to.

title.en: Elevating thoughts: only for tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every thought is a complete spiritual entity, sometimes a soul seeking a tikkun, which a tzaddik elevates to love or fear of Hashem. The Tanya warns that this is only for tzaddikim, whose foreign thoughts are not their own; someone whose thoughts are his own cannot elevate them.

title.en: No sadness: the klipah's war

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a person must not despair and cry out over his thoughts, but strengthen himself with joy in davening. The thought comes from the klipah in the left chamber of the heart, which wages a lifelong war with the G-dly soul, like two wrestlers.

title.en: Why the thoughts come during avodah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why bad thoughts come precisely when a person davens or resolves to improve, and answers that when the side of holiness strengthens itself, the other side fights back harder. He rejects the conclusion that such thoughts prove one is worthless.

title.en: Two souls, and the parable of the distracter

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that if a person had only one soul, a thought during davening would show something is wrong; but since he has two, the animal soul's thoughts say nothing about the davening. He brings the Tanya's parable of one who speaks with a friend while a wicked man stands opposite trying to distract him.

title.en: Bittul: 'you are nothing'

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that the way to deal with foreign thoughts is to nullify them, treating them as utterly nothing, like something dead. He tells stories of tzaddikim on this theme.

title.en: The great rule: ein od milvado

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls 'ein od milvado' a great rule in avodas Hashem: one who remembers that everything besides Hashem is nothing can win all his battles. One does not enter into conversation with the distracter, but strengthens himself in his kavanah.

title.en: The fly, and asking for mercy

summary.en: After a remark about the end of the Sefirah period, the Mashgiach brings that one of the yetzer hara's names is a fly, which keeps coming back however often it is chased away. When a thought will not leave, the Tanya's advice is to pour out one's heart to Hashem and ask for mercy on the G-dly soul.

title.en: Yahrzeit of Reb Shlomke of Zvil

summary.en: The Mashgiach marks the yahrzeit of Reb Shlomke of Zvil and tells how he said the gates of teshuvah would open before Moshiach, and how at the Kosel he pointed out houses that would be torn down, as happened in the Six Day War. He closes with l'chaim and wishes for yeshuos for Klal Yisroel.

catalogTitle: קיץ (for children): Be a Messenger of Hashem on Your Summer Vacation

oneLiner.en: Speaking to boys before summer vacation, the Mashgiach explains that Parshas Shlach is read just as the travel season begins to teach that every trip is a mission from Hashem, to be fulfilled like Yehoshua's successful spies and not like the spies of Moshe.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach contrasts two sets of spies: the meraglim Moshe sent in Parshas Shlach, who failed their mission and brought weeping on Tisha B'Av, and the spies Yehoshua sent to Yericho in the haftarah, who succeeded and are recorded with honor. He notes that the meraglim set out on Erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz, the week after Parshas Shlach, which is exactly when boys say goodbye to their rebbeim and leave for the summer. The Torah's message is that every person who travels is a shliach of Hashem, as the morning bracha 'hameichin mitzadei gaver' says: Hashem prepares every step. Everything in creation has a kind of life and waits for a Jew to come and do a mitzvah with it: a tree for a bracha on its apples or for Torah learned in its shade, water for a bracha, stones that wanted Yaakov to sleep on them, roads to Yerushalayim that mourn. He closes by telling the boys to be good messengers this summer.

en: The meraglim of Parshas Shlach were failed messengers who brought sorrow on Klal Yisrael, while Yehoshua's spies in the haftarah fulfilled their mission and brought success.
The Mashgiach says Parshas Shlach is read just before the summer travel begins because it teaches how to travel: whoever travels is a shliach of Hashem.
The bracha 'hameichin mitzadei gaver' means that Hashem prepares every step a person takes; wherever he goes, Hashem sends him there.
Everything in the world has some life and feeling, and waits for a Jew to come and do a mitzvah with it.
The Mashgiach tells the boys to remember on vacation that they are shluchim: to learn Torah, do mitzvos and behave like a Yid, so Hashem can be proud of them.

title.en: Two sets of spies

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Moshe's meraglim, who left the day before Rosh Chodesh Tammuz, returned on Tisha B'Av and are remembered with dishonor, with the spies Yehoshua sent to Yericho in the haftarah, who succeeded. He notes that the parsha read each week matches the events of that week.

title.en: Every traveler is Hashem's messenger

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that every year, right after Parshas Shlach, everyone says goodbye to his teachers and goes traveling, just as the meraglim did; this is the parsha's message. He asks the class the meaning of the bracha 'hameichin mitzadei gaver' and explains that Hashem prepares every step, so wherever a person goes he is sent there to do mitzvos.

title.en: All of creation waits for a mitzvah

summary.en: With the image of trees in the mountains waiting for a bracha on their apples or for a boy to learn Torah in their shade, and water waiting for a bracha, the Mashgiach teaches that everything is alive. He brings the stones that wanted Yaakov to sleep on them, the stones of the mizbeach that must not be shamed, and the roads to Yerushalayim that mourn.

title.en: Be a good messenger this summer

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the lesson to vacation: one goes places not for a suntan or baseball but as Hashem's shliach, to learn, make brachos with kavanah and do chesed. He closes by telling the boys to be successful messengers like Yehoshua's spies, and wishes them a good summer and a return to yeshivah.

catalogTitle: היום לא כל כך שכיח עתות רצון בשעת התפילה כי אוכלים מאכלות אסורות ויש טימטום הלב. עצה - לשבר את הגוף אבל רק בעתות מזומנים. כל אדם מעריך גופו כעיקר והנשמה כנטפל לו' אבל בצדיקים בהיפך.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 29, the Mashgiach explains why the heart can become as dull as stone, why this is so common today, and how one breaks the coarseness of the body so the light of the neshamah can take hold in it.

abstract.en: After opening words on the days of tashlumim after Shavuos, accepting the yoke of Heaven, and preparing all week for Shabbos, the Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter 29 on timtum halev, the heart that becomes like stone. He links it to the Gemara's reading of 'venitmeisem' as 'venitamtem': forbidden food blocks the heart, and he explains why kashrus today demands great care. A long digression on the taste and light that holiness puts into Shabbos follows, with stories of Kuzmir, the Satmar Rav and the Lechovitcher rebbetzin. Back in Tanya, he brings the Zohar's advice: wood that will not catch fire is chopped, so the body is broken at set times with a ruach nishbarah. He contrasts the beinoni, whose self is the body, with the tzaddik, whose self is the soul, explains Dovid's 'I am a worm and not a man', and ends with how to rebuke the body, through the story of a ger tzedek.

en: The Mashgiach explains that timtum halev, a dull heart that feels no joy in learning or davening, can come from forbidden food, as the Gemara reads 'venitmeisem' as 'venitamtem'.
He says this is common today because packaged food with countless ingredients and lesser hechsherim make kashrus hard, unlike the Ba'al HaTanya's time when food was cooked at home.
The Tanya's advice, from the Zohar, is to break the body: like wood that will not catch fire, it must be chopped so the light of the soul can take hold.
The body blocks the soul because of its coarseness, which comes from the strength of kelipas nogah, the animal soul that gives the body life.
In a beinoni the self is the body and the soul is something added to him, while in a tzaddik the soul is the person and the body is only his garment.
The Mashgiach says one must speak to the body and the yetzer hara and rebuke its chutzpah for rising over the neshamah and taking away the sweetness of Torah.

title.en: After Shavuos, before Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the seven days after Shavuos in which one can still make up the yom tov and take one's share in Torah, speaks of accepting the yoke of Heaven in a time of danger and of the protection Hashem gives through Sukkos, and then of preparing all week for Shabbos, the purpose of the week.

title.en: A heart like stone

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya on timtum halev, when the heart becomes like stone and one has no desire to daven, and brings the Gemara that forbidden food 'blocks' the heart, so that one no longer feels the joy of learning Torah.

title.en: Kashrus today and in the Tanya's time

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why a dulled heart is common today: packages of countless ingredients and lesser hechsherim, so one must be very careful about what one eats, as the Rambam explains on 'shomer piv'. In the Ba'al HaTanya's time food was cooked at home with yiras Shamayim and l'kavod Shabbos.

title.en: The taste and light of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Kuzmir chulent that tasted of Gan Eden because the Rebbe added beans 'l'kavod Shabbos kodesh', brings the Midrash on the special spice called Shabbos and on Shabbos being blessed with the light of a person's face, and describes how the Satmar Rav's face changed on Shabbos and each yom tov.

title.en: The Lechovitcher rebbetzin's candles

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Lechovitcher rebbetzin wept when her rich sister lit Shabbos candles, because she saw only a fire and not the light of Shabbos, adds that even electric light burns differently on Chol HaMoed, and brings Reb Mordechai of Lechovitch: one who does not work to feel the light of Shabbos will sit in Gan Eden like a log.

title.en: Wood that will not catch fire

summary.en: Back in the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that even in permitted things a person with a dull heart cannot hold back or sanctify himself, and brings the Zohar's advice of the head of the Heavenly yeshiva to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: wood that will not catch fire is chopped into small pieces, and so the body must be broken.

title.en: Why the soul's light does not take hold

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the soul wants to learn and daven with feeling, and one may understand Hashem's greatness with the mind, yet it does not reach the heart because of the body's coarseness, the strength of kelipas nogah. The remedy is to set times to humble oneself, for 'zivchei Elokim ruach nishbarah', a broken sitra achra.

title.en: Who is the 'I': beinoni and tzaddik

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks who a person means when he says 'I'. For the beinoni it is his body and animal soul, and the neshamah is like a drink poured into him, as in 'Elokai neshamah shenasata bi'. For the tzaddik the soul is the person and the body his garment, as Hillel went to 'do kindness' with his body as with a stranger.

title.en: A worm and not a man; truth by levels

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Dovid's words 'I am a worm and not a man': a worm does what it was created for, while a man who does not is worse than a worm. He then asks whether a love felt in davening that fades afterwards was untrue, and answers that truth has levels: for the beinoni that is his truth.

title.en: Rebuking the body; the ger tzedek's candle

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's advice to speak to the body and rebuke its chutzpah in darkening the light of the soul. He tells of Graf Potocki, the ger tzedek, who answered his executioners that the smell of an extinguished Shabbos candle was sweeter to him than all their pleasures, and says this is what one tells the yetzer hara.

catalogTitle: דברים שעושים טימטום הלב ואיך לתקן ולהזהר. בחינת האמת לפי מדריגתו. לפעמים אין התעוררות בשבת כי אז צריכים להיות במדריגה יותר זך. עצות כשיש טימטום הלב. למואס בגשמיות.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 29, the Mashgiach explains why a person suddenly cannot daven, why a higher level or a holier time demands a deeper teshuvah, and how to break the sitra achra through cheshbon hanefesh and seeing its nothingness before Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tanya chapter 29 on timtum halev, the closed heart that cannot daven. A hisorerus that fades after davening is still truth at a beinoni's level if it returns the next time. Sins of youth can block a person now, because above there is no time, and because each higher level needs a deeper teshuvah: Shabbos, Eretz Yisroel and every yahrzeit of a neshamah demand more than the weekday did. So a person who cannot daven should make a cheshbon hanefesh, like Dovid whose sin stood before him always. Even one without such sins can examine his wandering thoughts and his foolish dreams, as the Ba'al Shem Tov's Danzig story shows, yet without fear. He should then break himself with merirus, not atzvus, rebuke the sitra achra in his thoughts, and see that it is nullified before Hashem like darkness before light.

en: A beinoni's hisorerus that fades after davening is still truth at his level, as long as it comes back the next time.
Above there is no time, so a sin of long ago stands as if it were now, and teshuvah done once may not suffice for the present.
A higher level, whether in time (Shabbos), place (Eretz Yisroel) or the soul itself, demands a greater teshuvah, so a person may feel blocked exactly there.
When he cannot daven, a person should make a cheshbon hanefesh, perhaps Heaven wants to raise him higher and he must first do more teshuvah.
Even one without sins of youth can examine his thoughts and dreams, which show his soul does not ascend.
The breaking must come through merirus, which brings good counsel, and not through atzvus, which only puts one to sleep.
The sitra achra has no life of its own; it is nullified before Hashem like darkness before a lit candle.

candidateTopics: yahrzeit and the ascent of the soul

title.en: Timtum halev and truth by one's level

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the Tanya's counsel for a heart that is closed and cannot daven: to chop at it like a log that will not catch fire, and to make a cheshbon hanefesh. Reading on in chapter 29 and referring to chapter 13, he explains that truth has many levels, so a beinoni's arousal that returns each time is truth at his level.

title.en: Sins of youth, time, and the holiness of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that above there is no time, so a sin of youth stands as if committed now. With the parable of dressing for the street, a wedding and a king, he answers why one can daven on weekdays but not on Shabbos: Shabbos is the king's court and demands a greater teshuvah, and so too a holy place like Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The yahrzeit: a new judgment each year

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why on a yahrzeit people learn mishnayos and give tzedakah: each year the neshamah rises, and the cleansing that sufficed for last year's level is not enough for the next. In the same way a person in this world who is to rise higher needs a deeper teshuvah.

title.en: Cheshbon hanefesh and Dovid's sin before him

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one who cannot daven should ask why, and consider that Heaven may want to raise him. He brings Dovid's words that his sin is before him always: at every higher step one sees the sin anew and must do teshuvah again. Even one who did not sin can make a cheshbon, as some do daily, for thoughts fly through the mind by the thousand.

title.en: Thoughts, dreams, and davening without fear

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that thoughts not for the sake of Heaven belong to the other side, and tells the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of a man whose mind was in Danzig during davening. He then reads that foolish dreams show the soul does not ascend, and adds that this cheshbon must be made without fear, citing the tzaddikim's saying to think good and it will be good.

title.en: Breaking oneself: merirus, not atzvus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's counsel to sit and think that one is nothing, not an honest servant of Hashem, and so break himself. He stresses the difference between merirus, which brings good counsel, and atzvus, which only puts one to sleep; through this the swollen sitra achra that blocks his davening is broken.

title.en: Rebuking the sitra achra in thought

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's call to thunder at the yetzer hara: not aloud but in thought, asking how long it will hide the light of Hashem, who fills all worlds and is unchanged by creation. Seeing the truth, that all existence is nothing before Hashem, he illustrates with a story of the Ba'al haTanya at his passing.

title.en: Like darkness before light; despising physicality

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the sitra achra is nullified like darkness when a candle is lit, since its life is only sparks of kedushah it holds. He adds that darkness is itself a creation, and there is a holy darkness of tzimtzum, which is why the Tanya specifies physical light. He closes with the Tanya's counsel to despise physicality, which the yetzer uses to keep a person from davening.

catalogTitle: פרקי אבות The Evils of a תלמיד חכם with Bad מדות: צד א: כל הלומד תורה לשמה וכו' נקרא ריע, אהוב, אוהב 'את המקום וכו צד ב: משמח את המקום' משמח את הבריאות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Mishnah in Avos that one who learns Torah lishmah is a friend and beloved of Hashem and of people, and warns that Torah learning without good middos makes a person worse.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah that one who learns Torah lishmah is called a friend and beloved, loving Hashem and people. Every person longs to love and be loved, and the Torah channels this through two mitzvos: loving one's fellow and loving Hashem. All creatures deserve love because Hashem made them. Love between friends is the precondition for love of Hashem, as a story of two friends and a king shows, and shirah, like the malachim's, needs harmony. Through the Medrash on Shir HaShirim and a mashal of a car dealer he shows how priceless Hashem's love for a tzaddik is. He explains how love can be commanded, how Torah clothes a person in anavah and conditions him to be a tzaddik, with stories of tzaddikim kept from forbidden food. On the second side he stresses that learning without menschlichkeit makes a person worse, bringing the four animals with one kosher sign and the yetzer hara disguised as 'Yesh'.

en: The Mashgiach says every person has a built-in need to love and be loved, and the Torah turns it into avodas Hashem through the mitzvos of loving one's fellow and loving Hashem.
Love of creatures flows from the fact that Hashem created them, since He creates only what He likes; this reaches even a non-Jew, who has a tzelem Elokim, and even animals and insects.
Without love between friends there can be no love of Hashem, and shirah, which means harmony, is possible only among beings who love each other.
Hashem's love for one who learns Torah lishmah is beyond any price, and every Jew has this love in potential, which Torah learning brings out.
Torah lishmah clothes a person in anavah and prepares him to be a tzaddik, and Hashem guards tzaddikim from stumbling even unknowingly.
The Mashgiach stresses that learning without being a mensch makes a person worse, and that a talmid chacham must be seen by people as a decent human being.

title.en: The Mishnah and the human need to love

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Mishnah that one who learns Torah lishmah is called a friend and beloved, and explains that tzaddikim use the inborn desire to love and be loved for its true purpose. He explains why one must love all creatures, even a non-Jew and even insects, because Hashem made them.

title.en: Love of friends and the king who joined

summary.en: The Mashgiach says there can be no love of Hashem without love between friends, and tells of two friends in Rome, each ready to die for the other, whom the king asked to take into their friendship. He adds that malachim can sing shirah only because they love each other, since shirah means harmony.

title.en: Malachim, the classroom, and the shirah at the Yam Suf

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts competition in a classroom with the malachim who give each other permission to sing out of love. At the splitting of the sea the Yidden sang shirah in place of the malachim, so they too needed that love, which is the key to a connection with Hashem.

title.en: A love no wealth can buy

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Shir HaShirim that many waters cannot extinguish the love between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and the Medrash of a tzaddik's coffin that floated in the air. With a mashal of a customer offering a few dollars for an expensive car, he explains why offering all one's wealth for that love would be scorned, and says one reaches it through Torah lishmah.

title.en: Can love be commanded; anavah as a garment

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the bochurim's question how the Torah can command a feeling: every Jew has the love in potential, and Torah lishmah makes it flare up. He then explains that Torah clothes a person in anavah, which is like a coat that can be put on and taken off, and that it takes da'as to know when to use it.

title.en: Torah prepares a person to be a tzaddik

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Torah lishmah prepares a person to be a tzaddik even in matters beyond his control, such as forbidden food that dulls his feeling for kedushah. Since one cannot be careful enough, tzaddikim need siyata dishmaya, and he tells of a tzaddik who sensed any doubt in his food and would not eat a questionable piece of chicken.

title.en: The pancake that squirted

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a gadol who, at a Rav's lunch, became absorbed in pilpul and did not eat a pancake that turned out to have been made with butter in a fleishig pan. He said it was not ruach hakodesh: the hot fat squirted into his face while he learned, so he concluded it could not be kosher.

title.en: A Rebbe and the untoveled dishes

summary.en: The Mashgiach retells a story he heard from an elderly Yerushalmi in his shul in Williamsburg: a Rebbe in Yerushalayim came to eat at a beardless yerei shamayim, did not touch the fish, and discovered that the dishes, borrowed from a chassid with a beard and peyos, had not been toveled. The Rebbe told the host what each would be asked in the next world.

title.en: The gabbai and the knife

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story he heard from Mr. Singer, a man in the shul of his youth: a Rebbe's gabbai, a great tzaddik, stayed with Mr. Singer's father for Shabbos, and refused a new knife that the boy had claimed to tovel but had not, because the river was frozen. The Mashgiach concludes that Torah conditions a person to be a tzaddik and gives him all the help he needs.

title.en: Gladdening people: the chassidim's love

summary.en: On the second side the Mashgiach returns to the Mishnah: one who learns Torah lishmah gladdens Hashem and people. He brings a letter printed at the end of the Noam Elimelech in which a man describes to his father-in-law, who feared the chassidim, how they love each other like brothers, so that one cannot tell whose children are whose. He then notes the Gemara's harsh words about learning not lishmah.

title.en: Power misused: the four animals

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Torah to a great power that blesses when used well and destroys when misused, and notes that when people are pleased with a person Hashem is pleased with him. He brings the Medrash that the four animals with one kosher sign stand for the four exiles, and explains that a good sign used for evil makes them worse, as with one who learns without good middos.

title.en: Rachamim after the ir hanidachas

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in this week's parsha that after destroying an ir hanidachas Hashem will give rachamim, and the Ohr HaChaim's account of the king's executioners who said killing gives them pleasure. He applies it: if one is not a mensch, his learning makes him worse, and a talmid chacham must let others live as long as they do no harm.

title.en: The yetzer hara called 'Yesh'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a parable: the yetzer hara, the original serpent, complained that nobody listens to him because everyone recognizes him, so he changed his name, finally to 'Yesh', and went around the batei midrash and yeshivos, so that the more people learned the more of a 'yesh' they became. He concludes that Torah is meant to bring anavah and make a person a mensch, and that a real oved Hashem never has bad middos.

title.en: Before Moshiach: throwing off restraint

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how just before Moshiach people want to throw off every moral restraint and do whatever they want, citing the Gemara that before Moshiach chutzpah will increase and the generation will be like a dog. Against this he praises the refined speech and conduct of a talmid chacham as the Rambam defines it.

title.en: Closing

catalogTitle: הקדמה למזמור שיר ליום השבת

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that in Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos it is Shabbos itself that sings to Hashem, and that our weekly Shabbos sings to the great Shabbos of the future, when all of history will be heard as one harmony.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens a series on the meaning of the tefillos, saying that knowing what the words mean can bring warmth into davening, and begins with Shabbos and the chapter Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos. Every chapter of Tehillim has one theme running through it like a string through pearls; here the theme is that Shabbos itself sings. Creation was made in seven days like the seven notes of music, and only when the seventh day completes the seven-stringed harp can there be song; so too the seventh sea, the seventh land and King David are singers. From a Midrash that Adam said this chapter after learning the power of teshuvah, the Mashgiach explains Shabbos and yovel as the return of everything to its root. Our Shabbos sings to the great Shabbos of the future, when the world will see that all of history, even the suffering of tzaddikim and of Klal Yisrael, was one harmony.

en: Every chapter of Tehillim has one theme threaded through all its verses, so the Mashgiach first states a chapter's theme before translating its verses.
Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos does not mean a song about Shabbos but a song that Shabbos itself sings to Hashem.
Music needs all seven notes; the world, created in seven days, has its song only once Shabbos completes the seven-stringed harp.
Shabbos, like yovel, means the return of everything to its root, which is why the Midrash ties this chapter to teshuvah.
Our weekly Shabbos is a small Shabbos singing to the great Shabbos of the future, the day that is entirely Shabbos.
People cannot see how the suffering of tzaddikim and the success of the wicked fit together, but from Hashem's height it is all one harmony.

candidateTopics: teshuvah and return to the root

title.en: Why learn the meaning of the tefillos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah's mitzvah is to daven with the heart, and that in weak generations knowing the meaning of the words can bring warmth into davening. He begins with the Shabbos davening, notes that Lecha Dodi is a later custom, and that the Shulchan Aruch speaks of accepting Shabbos with Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos.

title.en: Tehillim as King David's portion in Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every person has his own portion in the Torah, and the whole book of Tehillim is King David's portion, even chapters that Adam or Moshe said. He then explains that each chapter has one theme running through it like a string through pearls, so he will first give each chapter's content.

title.en: Shabbos sings: the seven notes of creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the chapter is called a song of Shabbos when it says nothing about Shabbos, and answers that Shabbos itself sings. Through the seven 'kol' of Mizmor l'Dovid, the seven-stringed harp of the Beis Hamikdash and the seven notes of music, he explains that the world's harmony becomes song only when Shabbos completes the seven days.

title.en: The seventh is always the singer

summary.en: From a Midrash on the seventh day, the seventh sea and the seventh land, the Mashgiach shows that the seventh always sings: the Kinneret, Eretz Yisrael, the zemer among the animals, and King David as the seventh of the ushpizin. He brings the Lechovitcher's saying about a Jew who can sing and does not sing on Shabbos, and the custom to sing Kel Adon with a tune.

title.en: Shabbos, teshuvah and yovel: return to the root

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Adam said this chapter when he heard from Kayin the power of teshuvah, and asks what Shabbos has to do with teshuvah. He explains that everything must return to its root, as in Koheles, the Maharal and the Ramban on yovel, and that Shabbos and above all the yovel bring back even the furthest Jew.

title.en: This year's yovel and the Shabbos of the future

summary.en: In passing, the Mashgiach says that by the accepted reckoning this year, 5755, is a yovel year, discusses how the fiftieth year is counted, and mentions kavanos of the mekubalim for it. He then explains that in Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos the lower Shabbos sings to the higher one, the day that is entirely Shabbos, and expresses the hope that this year will be a time of favor for the redemption.

title.en: The questions of history and their tikkun

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the questions people ask on Hashem because of the suffering of Jews, from the Churban through the Crusades, the Inquisition and the six million, and says that we cannot answer but justify Hashem's judgment. He brings what the sefarim reveal: the martyrs of Tach v'Tat and the Asarah Harugei Malchus as rectifications of earlier sins, that Hashem never forgives a Jew's blood, and that before Moshiach souls are gathered into one generation for their tikkun.

title.en: Seeing the whole picture: the chapter's message

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the chapter's verses on Hashem's deep thoughts and His being on high, and gives the mashal of a fly on a Rembrandt painting that sees only a black spot. He tells his listeners to sing with Shabbos at the Shabbos table as a taste of the future Shabbos, and sums up the chapter with its last verse, explaining a word written without a vav as the hidden connection that is missing from our sight.

catalogTitle: מזמור שיר ליום השבת

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos as the song the world of tikkun will sing over all of history, in which the good times and the dark times together make one harmony, like the ten-stringed asor and the sad-toned navel.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by calling Shabbos the return, the yovel, and links it to Yerushalayim, the Shabbos of place, whose letters he finds in 'shir l'yom'. He explains why Shabbos is the day for 'tov lehodos': on Shabbos a Jew is equipped with extra powers to praise Hashem. On 'lehagid baboker chasdecha ve'emunascha baleilos' he brings Chavakuk, who based all the mitzvos on emunah, and a story of souls weary of gilgulim who were told to hold onto emunah. 'Alei asor' leads to the kinor of seven, eight and ten strings and the Sfas Emes on the new note of Moshiach's world. Through the piano's white and black keys he shows that joyful and sad times together form the melody of history. Rebbe Nachman, the Chazon Ish's tailor parable and stories of Reb Itzikl of Pshevorsk show that only the end reveals the meaning, and 'ki simachtani' closes it.

en: Shabbos is the Shabbos of time and Yerushalayim the Shabbos of place, so the words 'shir l'yom' share the letters of Yerushalayim.
Praising Hashem is an obligation every day, but on Shabbos a Jew is better equipped for it, with the neshamah yeseirah and freedom from physical concerns.
In the dark times before Moshiach the main demand of a Jew is emunah, knowing that everything is hashgacha pratis.
The kinor of the Mikdash had seven strings, Moshiach's will have eight and the final one ten, because the world to come will be too wonderful to be sung with seven notes.
Like the white and black keys of a piano, the good and bad times of history play together in one harmony, and the whole of history is Hashem's niggun.
Only at the end can one see why each painful event was needed, as the stories of Reb Itzikl of Pshevorsk show.

candidateTopics: the kinor of seven, eight and ten strings
music and the days of Moshiach
good and bad times as one harmony

title.en: Shabbos and Yerushalayim: the place of return

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Shabbos the yovel and the return, explains the name Shabbos Hagadol, and shows that what exists in time exists in place: Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of geography, which is why 'shir l'yom' has its letters.

title.en: Why Shabbos is the day to praise

summary.en: On 'tov lehodos' the Mashgiach brings the Radak and asks why Shabbos is singled out when one must praise Hashem always; he answers that on Shabbos a Jew is equipped with extra powers, and so Shabbos davening adds mizmorim and Nishmas.

title.en: Chavakuk, emunah and the weary souls

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Chavakuk based all the mitzvos on emunah, tells of souls weary of endless gilgulim who were told by Hashem to grab onto emunah, and explains 'emunascha baleilos' as holding onto emunah in the dark times of hester panim.

title.en: Alei asor: the strings of the kinor

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the song of Shabbos as a look back over the journey of exile, then brings Rav Hirsch and the Gemara on the kinor of seven, eight and ten strings, explains the octave, and speaks of the wisdom of music.

title.en: The eighth note and the ten maamaros

summary.en: Following the Sfas Emes, the Mashgiach explains that Moshiach's world will need a new eighth note, illustrating with phone-number combinations, and ties the ten strings to the ten maamaros, when Jews will rise above the angels.

title.en: Asor and navel, white keys and black keys

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads asor as richness and navel as withering, describes the piano's white and black keys, says that inventions spread over the world come with hashgacha, and explains white as chesed and black as din through doctors' and Kohanim's white clothing.

title.en: History as one symphony

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies alei asor and alei navel to the history of every nation and every Jew: bad times are part of the harmony, so one blesses on the bad as on the good and says gam zu letovah, and 'higayon b'chinor' means to contemplate the whole world as Hashem's instrument.

title.en: Every life a niggun; the tailor's silk

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rebbe Nachman that every person's life is a niggun, then the Chazon Ish's answer about the six million with the parable of a tailor cutting silk, and points to the rebuilding of Torah in Eretz Yisrael while the garment is still being sewn.

title.en: Reb Itzikl of Pshevorsk and 'ki simachtani'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of Reb Itzikl of Pshevorsk healing a melamed through anger, and of his refusal of Russian citizenship, which sent his followers to Siberia and saved them; he concludes that we are blind until the end, and with 'ki simachtani' that the wonders we do understand let us trust those we don't.

catalogTitle: כי שמחתני ה' בפעלך וכו'

oneLiner.en: Going through Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos, the Mashgiach explains that on Shabbos a Jew sees the harmony of creation and rejoices even in what he cannot understand, knowing that the wicked flourish like grass only to wither while Klal Yisrael, rooted in unity and in the 'eighth' level above nature, endures forever.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the second half of Psalm 92. At the end of days every question will be answered; on Shabbos, freed from the week's toil, a person looks at the harmony of creation, sings, and concludes that what he does not understand also has deep answers. Following the Rambam, contemplating creation leads to love of Hashem. The 'ish ba'ar' knows he cannot understand Hashem's ways; the fool turns this into a question about why the wicked prosper. The wicked are like grass that sprouts first and withers first, as a story of a Jew forced off a plane that later crashed illustrates. Hashem is 'marom', beyond reach; empires vanished while Jews remained. The Ba'al Shem Tov teaches that seeing Hashem behind every enemy sweetens the judgments. Evil belongs to division, Shabbos to unity; the world decays since Adam's sin, but Klal Yisrael, like the Chanukah oil, belongs to the eternal 'eighth', and the tzaddik grows slowly like a palm and lasts forever.

en: On Shabbos, free from the week's labor, a person contemplates the harmony of creation and sings, and from what he sees he concludes that what he does not understand also has deep answers.
The 'ish ba'ar' at least knows that Hashem's ways are beyond him, while the fool takes his own lack of understanding as a question against Hashem.
The wicked are like grass, the first to sprout in spring and the first to wither, so their success is only for their eventual destruction.
The great empires that oppressed the Jews, Egypt, Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome, came to nothing, while the Jews remained.
Everything holy is unity and everything opposed to holiness is division; Shabbos is the secret of oneness, so the wicked, who belong to division, cannot endure it.
Since Adam's sin everything in the seven days of creation must end, but the Jewish soul belongs to the 'eighth', above nature, and will live to see the eternal Shabbos.
The tzaddik is not like grass but like a palm and a cedar: he grows slowly and lasts forever.

title.en: Ki simachtani: singing on Shabbos about creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that at the end of days all questions will be answered, and that on Shabbos, freed from the week's toil, a person looks at the beauty and harmony of creation and sings. From what he sees he understands that Hashem's thoughts are very deep, and that what he does not understand also has brilliant answers.

title.en: Ish ba'ar, the fool, and the wicked like grass

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that contemplating creation leads to love of Hashem, then explains that the 'ish ba'ar' knows he cannot understand Hashem's conduct while the fool asks the old question why the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer. He answers with the parable of grass, which sprouts first in spring and withers first at summer's end.

title.en: The seat on the plane from Morocco

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that the success of a rasha can be his downfall and the troubles of a tzaddik his success, and tells of a Jewish businessman who was forced to give up his seat on a plane from Morocco to an Arab sheikh; the plane crashed, and the man made a seudas hodaah.

title.en: Hashem is marom; empires come and go

summary.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes 'gavoha', high but rising from the ground, from 'marom', high and detached like a cloud, and says Hashem's ways are marom, beyond reach. On 'ki hinei oyvecha' he shows how Egypt, Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome vanished like waves breaking on the shore, while the Jews remained.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov: Hashem behind every enemy

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that every trouble a Jew suffers from people is Hashem in disguise; when a Jew recognizes this the judgments are sweetened and the kelipah breaks, and this is how he reads 'ki hinei oyvecha'. He then explains that holiness is unity and its opposite is division, bringing Chazal's contrast between Yaakov's 'nefesh' and Esav's 'nafshos'.

title.en: Yom echad, the second day, and Shabbos as oneness

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash on why the first day is called 'yom echad', and explains that on the second day division, Gehinnom and evil were created, connecting this to the Gemara on pairs. Shabbos is 'raza d'echad', so the wicked, who belong to division, cannot exist on it and are scattered, while Klal Yisrael's horn is raised.

title.en: Everything decays since Adam; the eighth above nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that through Adam's sin decay came upon all of creation, so everything in the seven days of creation must end, but not the Jewish people, who will live to see the eternal Shabbos. He brings the Maharal's concept of the 'eighth world' above the limits of the seven of nature, and the Gemara that the harp of the Beis HaMikdash had seven strings and that of Moshiach will have eight.

title.en: Wine and oil, Torah and the Chanukah oil

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah was given on the fiftieth day, entering the eighth week, because it comes from heaven. Wine, whose value is seventy, belongs to the seven, while oil, from the word 'shemonah', rises above every liquid and does not spoil; the Chanukah oil, which was not consumed, lasted eight days. That oil, revealed to Yaakov, is 'shemen ra'anan', the endless existence of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Tishmanah oznai and the tzaddik like a palm

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the nations look at the Jew and plan his end, but Klal Yisrael has a hidden ruach hakodesh that hears 'from behind the curtain' that it will outlive them, as Jews sang in the camps. He closes with the tzaddik who is not like quick grass but like a palm and a cedar, growing slowly and lasting forever.

catalogTitle: דרשה בבית האסורים: English: Freedom in Prison. אידיש: גודל תענוג השכינה מעבודה בעמקי הקליפות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the light Hashem created on the twenty-fifth of Elul is true freedom, the freedom from the yetzer hara to serve Hashem, and that even from the lowest places a Jew can crown Hashem as King.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the twenty-fifth of Elul, the day the world was created, and the words 'Yehi or', 'let there be light', which he says are repeated each year on this day. Light, he explains, means happiness and contentment, and above all liberty. Dovid HaMelech calls prisoners those who sit in darkness, but the greatest imprisonment is to be bound by the yetzer hara; the whole world, in his words, is a big prison, because people who think they are free must obey their bad passions. When Hashem said 'let there be light' He meant freedom to serve Him, which every person inwardly desires. The Mashgiach speaks of the awaited Rosh Hashanah when all mankind will be free to serve Hashem, and blesses his listeners. He then turns to Yiddish and teaches that service from the lowest places brings great joy above, and that a Jew should proclaim 'HaMelech' wherever he is.

en: Each year on the twenty-fifth of Elul, the day of creation, the creation and the 'Yehi or' are repeated.
Light means happiness and contentment, and its most precious form is liberty.
The greatest imprisonment is being a prisoner of the yetzer hara, and in this sense the whole world is a big prison.
'Let there be light' meant freedom to serve Hashem and follow the good inclinations every person carries inside.
The world awaits a Rosh Hashanah when all mankind will be free, subservient to no will but Hashem's.

title.en: The light of creation is liberty

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the twenty-fifth of Elul, when the world was created and Hashem said 'Yehi or', and explains that light means happiness and above all liberty. He says the greatest prison is the yetzer hara, and that the whole world is a big prison of people who think they are free.

title.en: Freedom to serve Hashem and the awaited Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'let there be light' meant freedom to serve Hashem, which every human being inwardly desires, and speaks of the coming Rosh Hashanah when all mankind will be free of the yetzer hara. He blesses the listeners and announces that he will continue in Yiddish.

title.en: Serving Hashem from the depths

summary.en: In a Yiddish discourse, the Mashgiach speaks of the joy above when a Jew serves Hashem from the lowest places, among idol worshippers and outside Eretz Yisrael. On Rosh Hashanah, he says, a Jew should proclaim 'HaMelech' wherever he is, since even a prison is a place to serve Hashem.

catalogTitle: צדיק כתמר וכו'

oneLiner.en: Learning the end of Mizmor Shir leYom HaShabbos and the start of Hashem Malach, the Mashgiach explains that the tzaddik flourishes like the date palm and the cedar, and that when Moshiach comes everyone will see that all of Hashem's hidden din was really rachamim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the wicked, who sprout like grass and wither at the end of the season, with the tzaddik who flourishes like the date palm. A fruit tree does not grow tall because its strength goes into its fruit, while the cedar grows tall but gives no fruit; the tzaddik who gives his strength to his students is promised siyata dishmaya and has both, as shown from the chassidim rishonim and the Chasam Sofer's children. He stresses being planted in the right place, bringing the Rambam and the Kuzari, and explains that Klal Yisrael will blossom only when the galus ends. 'Lehagid ki yashar Hashem' means that in the future all suffering will be seen as good; he illustrates midas hadin through the combinations of the Name in Nissan, Teves and Tammuz. On Hashem Malach he explains that Hashem's apparent aloofness is only a garment, with the Ba'al Shem Tov's worm story, and that in the mixed-up world of 'tevel' Hashem still holds everything firm.

en: The wicked are like grass that flourishes quickly and withers at the reckoning, while the tzaddik is like the date palm that grows slowly but endures forever.
A tzaddik who gives his strength to his students does not lose by it: Hashem gives him siyata dishmaya, so he is both fruitful like the palm and tall like the cedar.
A person must be planted in the right place, among tzaddikim and ehrliche Yidden, to grow; Klal Yisrael too could not blossom in galus.
'Lehagid ki yashar Hashem' teaches that in the days of Moshiach it will be revealed that all the din Jews suffered was rachamim inside and for their good.
Hashem's apparent aloofness, 'gei'us lavesh', is only a garment; underneath He watches over every smallest creature with hashgachah pratis.
The world is called 'tevel', a mixture in which one cannot see clearly, yet Hashem holds it firm and sometimes sends a flash of open miracles.

candidateTopics: the future revelation that din was rachamim
combinations of the Name Havayah in the months

title.en: The palm and the grass

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens the passuk 'tzaddik katamar yifrach' against the earlier verses about the wicked who sprout like grass. He explains that a fruit tree stays low because its strength goes into its fruit while the cedar grows tall without fruit, and compares this to teachers who give their strength to their students.

title.en: Giving to others costs nothing

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the tzaddik is promised siyata dishmaya so he does not lose by teaching others, bringing the chassidim rishonim who davened nine hours a day and the Chasam Sofer, whose student answered his worry about his children with 'kol hayom chonen umalveh'. The tzaddik has both the palm's fruit and the cedar's height.

title.en: Planted in the house of Hashem

summary.en: After Rav Hirsch's reading, the Mashgiach explains 'shesulim b'veis Hashem': the tzaddik is planted in the beis medrash, like the golden trees of the Beis Hamikdash. He stresses being in the right place, with the Rambam and the Kuzari's tree that needs its own soil, and explains that Klal Yisrael will blossom anew at the end of galus, 'od yenuvun beseivah'.

title.en: Lehagid ki yashar Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls 'lehagid ki yashar Hashem' the summary of the chapter: it looks unfair that tzaddikim suffer and the wicked succeed, but later it will be revealed that everything was for Klal Yisrael's good. He brings Reb Nachum that even the nations will then grasp that Jews in galus were happier than they, with 'az yimalei schok pinu'.

title.en: Din and rachamim in the months

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that in the future only 'hatov vehameitiv' will be said, since din will be seen as a garment over rachamim. He explains that each month has its own combination of the Name Havayah: Nissan, from 'yismechu hashamayim', is pure chessed, while Teves is a month of din connected to Esav, softened by the Chanukah lights.

title.en: Tammuz: the Name written backwards

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tammuz, whose combination comes from 'vechol zeh einenu shoveh li' fully backwards, holds the harshest din, worse than Av. Yet when Moshiach comes it will be seen that Havayah was always straight, and the troubles of all the generations will be understood as 'ki yashar Hashem'.

title.en: Hashem Malach: the garment of pride

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem Malach continues the previous chapter, which is why they are said together at Kabbalas Shabbos, and that looking back from Moshiach one will say Hashem 'malach', He always reigned. With a mashal of a proud man who ignores small people, he explains that Hashem only seems aloof, as the apikorsim claim, but 'hamashpili lir'os' He watches over everything.

title.en: The worm and the hidden face

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of a breeze Hashem sent for a suffering worm, and explains that 'gei'us lavesh' is a garment over a garment, hester within hester. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's mashal of a child in the forest who does not see his father watching, and a deeper hiding where he does not even know.

title.en: Af tikon tevel: the world holds firm

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'af tikon tevel bal timot': people fear the world will be destroyed, as the Dor Haflagah built a tower to hold up the sky, but Hashem watches over it. He explains that 'tevel' means a mixture, a world where one does not see clearly, yet at times like Chanukah and Purim Hashem sends a flash of light, 'he'iru verakav tevel'.

catalogTitle: ה' מלך גאות לבש

oneLiner.en: Learning Tehillim 93, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem's kingship is hidden throughout the galus, and that when Moshiach comes it will be revealed that He was always King and everything was for the good of the Jewish people.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Tehillim 93, which continues Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos and speaks of the time of Moshiach, when it will be revealed retroactively that Hashem was always King. Following the Ramban's principle that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, he explains that the akeidah's real test was not the slaughter itself but Avraham's unanswered question against Hashem's promise; this is the last test of our generation too. He reads the psalm verse by verse: the rivers and the breakers of the sea are the kingdoms that rose against Israel, and Hashem on high is mightier. A second reading, from a Midrash on the lower waters and the Yismach Moshe on Al naharos Bavel, has the rivers weeping with Israel and hoping. Eidosecha are the prophets or Klal Yisrael itself, faithful to Hashem's house. He ends with Chad Gadya and with Tehillim 29, where all beauty and strength are ascribed to Hashem, unlike Greek and American culture.

en: Hashem malach refers to the time of Moshiach, when it will be revealed that Hashem was always King, even through the hiding of the galus.
The test of the akeidah was that Avraham had a question against Hashem's promise and was not given the answer; this is also the last test of the present generation.
The rivers and the breakers of the sea in the psalm are the kingdoms and empires that tried to drown Israel, and Hashem on high is mightier than all of them.
In a second reading, the rivers weep over the Beis Hamikdash together with Israel, and the Jewish people's hope to return is itself their strength.
Klal Yisrael are Hashem's witnesses: their very existence, after all the kingdoms have vanished, testifies that Hashem exists and gave the Torah.
Tehillim 29 teaches that all beauty and strength must be ascribed to Hashem, against the Greek culture of deifying strength and beauty that rules America today.

korbanos and the elevation of creation

title.en: Hashem malach and the test of the akeidah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tehillim 93 continues the Shabbos psalm and speaks of the time of Moshiach, when Hashem's hidden kingship will be revealed. With the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, he turns to the akeidah as the last and hardest test and asks why it was a test at all.

title.en: A question without an answer

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham's real test was that his madreigos were taken from him and he had a question against Hashem's promise, and he was not given the answer that every child learning Chumash with Rashi knows. This is the test of our generation, full of questions; when Moshiach comes all will be answered, and it will be seen that Hashem was always King.

title.en: The rivers and the breakers are the kingdoms

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains nachon kis'acha me'az: Hashem was always King, but the world, olam, is from he'elem, hiddenness. Following the commentators, the rising rivers are the kingdoms that oppressed Israel in galus and the breakers of the sea are the great empires, yet Hashem on high is mightier and they will come to their downfall.

title.en: The weeping of the lower waters

summary.en: The Mashgiach offers another reading from a Midrash: the lower waters cried that they were not close to the King, and Hashem promised them nisuch hamayim and the salt on the mizbe'ach, through which all of creation is brought close through korbanos. After the churban the waters wept again, and he brings the Yismach Moshe on gam bachinu: the rivers of Bavel wept, and Israel wept too.

title.en: The rivers' cry and Israel's hope

summary.en: On this reading, the rivers raise their voice in weeping over the Beis Hamikdash and Israel identifies with them. Mishberei yam is read as hope, like Rashi's reading of shever in Mitzrayim, and the hope that Hashem on high will rebuild His house is itself Israel's strength and comfort in galus.

title.en: Eidosecha ne'emnu me'od

summary.en: With Rashi, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem's witnesses are the prophets, whose promises of redemption we trust, and that the whole galus is a journey to Hashem's house, like the masa'os in the wilderness. He then reads the witnesses as Klal Yisrael itself, whose existence testifies to Hashem, and explains ne'emnu as firm and loyal, and the form eidosecha as pointing to the weak sheep among seventy wolves.

title.en: L'orech yamim and Chad Gadya

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that l'orech yamim refers to the day that is entirely Shabbos and to the third Beis Hamikdash, which will never again be destroyed, when Hashem remains alone with His people. He brings the Chasam Sofer's reading of Chad Gadya: kingdom after kingdom swallows the little goat, and in the end Hashem remains with His Chad Gadya.

title.en: Havu laShem: ascribing all strength to Hashem

summary.en: Turning to Tehillim 29 sung at Kabbalas Shabbos, the Mashgiach recalls its seven kolos, matching the seven days of creation and the seven strings of the harp, and explains that Shabbos is malchus, when everything good and strong is ascribed to Hashem. He contrasts this with Greek culture that deifies strength and beauty, explains that Edom includes all the earlier kingdoms, and brings Reb Feivel Mendlowitz's remark that the leviathan's stomach is in America.

catalogTitle: מזמור לדוד הבו לה' בני אלים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Mizmor l'David, Havu laShem bnei elim, as the chapter of bitul, giving all strength and beauty back to Hashem, and shows why this is how one receives Shabbos, the day of Hashem's kingship.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the place of Mizmor l'David at the end of Kabbalas Shabbos and the Gemara that ties its eighteen Names and seven 'voices' to the eighteen weekday brachos and the seven of Shabbos. Following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, he reads the chapter as a call to the mighty to credit all strength and beauty to Hashem and to hear 'the voice of Hashem' inside them. Since bitul is the attribute of malchus, which belongs to Shabbos and to David HaMelech, this is the chapter for receiving Shabbos. He explains that bitul is the purpose of creation, to be completed when the whole world recognizes Hashem, and illustrates it with stories of tzaddikim. True humility, he says, is joy and nullification, not depression, shown by Yishmael's teshuvah and by Yosef joining his brothers' minyan. He ends with the Gemara and Rashi on the verses and with Hashem's voice in destruction and rebuilding.

en: The Gemara links the eighteen Names in this chapter to the eighteen weekday brachos and its seven 'voices' to the seven brachos of Shabbos, so the chapter stands on the border between weekday and Shabbos.

Following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, the chapter tells the mighty and the beautiful that their strength and beauty are Hashem's, and that one should hear 'the voice of Hashem' speaking out of every strength and beauty in the world.
Bitul to Hashem is the attribute of malchus, which is revealed on Shabbos and embodied by David HaMelech, and this is why the chapter is used to receive Shabbos.
Bitul is the purpose of a person's service and of all creation, as Shabbos is the purpose of creation, and it will be completed when the whole world recognizes Hashem's kingship.
True humility is not going about broken and depressed but being happy that one has so great a Creator and nullifying oneself to His will.
Hachna'ah, yielding to Hashem, to tzaddikim, to friends and to every creature, includes everything, and its truest form is reached on Shabbos.
The same 'voice of Hashem' heard in the world's beauty is in its destruction too, and Hashem can rebuild what was destroyed and make even the wilderness bloom.
