title.en: Mizmor l'David between weekday and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach places Mizmor l'David after Lecha Dodi in Kabbalas Shabbos and brings the Gemara linking its eighteen Names to the eighteen weekday brachos and its seven 'voices' to the seven brachos of Shabbos. He notes that receiving the extra soul of Shabbos fully requires immersing in a mikvah erev Shabbos.

title.en: Rav Hirsch: give all strength to Hashem

summary.en: Following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, the Mashgiach reads the chapter as a call to the strong and the beautiful to credit their might and honor to Hashem and bow before Him. He explains 'the voice of Hashem is in strength, in beauty': in every power and every beautiful thing one should hear Hashem speaking.

title.en: Why this chapter receives Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that bitul is the attribute of malchus, revealed on Shabbos and embodied by David HaMelech, the seventh of the ushpizin. He brings the Gemara that Avraham, Moshe and David each made themselves nothing, and the Chasam Sofer's point that father, teacher and king all did so, and concludes that Shabbos is the day to proclaim oneself Hashem's creation.

title.en: Bitul, the purpose of creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the usual commentators' reading of Havu laShem, then explains that bitul is the purpose of man and of creation, to be completed in the days of Moshiach when all the world recognizes Hashem, as one prays on Rosh Hashanah. He tells how Rav Yisroel of Vizhnitz twirled a window-shade string during Shemoneh Esrei, praying that even the string should know it was created by Hashem.

title.en: What true humility is

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Maggid of Mezritch sending for the Baal HaTanya, who was singing 'veyeda kol pa'ul' at his shtender. He then explains that humility is not depression but joyful bitul, that a tzaddik may praise himself while being nothing in his own eyes, and tells of the youngest son of Rav Mordechai of Chernobyl, who took 'nothing' as his share.

title.en: Yishmael and Yosef: the sign of hachna'ah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Yishmael's teshuvah was seen in his yielding to Yitzchak, and brings the Igra deKallah's answer to why Yosef never wrote to his father: the brothers had bound the Shechinah by an oath, and Yosef himself joined to make their minyan. He concludes that the heart of Yiddishkeit is bitul to Hashem, to tzaddikim, to friends and to every creature.

title.en: Shabbos, Yerushalayim and seeing Hashem in everything

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos, when a Jew produces nothing, is the day to reach bitul, and brings the Baal HaTanya that true prostration needs the holiness of Yerushalayim. He ties Rav Hirsch's reading to the Baal Shem Tov's teaching of seeing Hashem in food, beauty and every object, and tells how Rav Eizikel of Komarna saw only holy Names before his eyes.

title.en: The three havu and the first three brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that bnei elim are the children of the Avos and the Gemara that derives the first three brachos of Shemoneh Esrei from the three 'havu'. He brings the Radak that the waters are the nations, and the Gemara that 'Kel hakavod hir'im' is the source of the nineteenth bracha against the wicked.

title.en: The voice of Hashem in destruction and rebuilding

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the breaking of the cedars of Lebanon as Hashem humbling the mighty nations, and with Rav Hirsch teaches that the same voice of Hashem heard in beauty is in destruction and in the shifting of nations' borders. He ends with 'kol Hashem yachil midbar': Hashem can make even the wilderness bloom, as Midbar Kadesh became a great house of learning.

catalogTitle: דרשה לנשים: Shidduchim - of Sublime Origin; צניעות & חנוכה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a shidduch is so heavenly that it stands above time and space, and that Chanukah, whose miracle came through Yehudis, is a time for women to strengthen tznius.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Torah records kfitzas haderech, a miraculous shortening of the road, only twice: when Eliezer went to find a kallah for Yitzchak and when Yaakov went to find his own. Everything in this world happens in time and place, but Shamayim is above both, and a zivug is a heavenly creation. This is why the bas kol that announces a match forty days before conception errs again and again, why the tenth of the ten utterances of creation begins with 'lo tov', and why, as the Tzemach Tzedek writes, the shadchan's small untruth is needed to bring the match down into this world. Turning to Chanukah, the Mashgiach explains that women were the core of the miracle through Yehudis, which is why they refrain from work while the candles burn. Following the Chasam Sofer, their not lighting their own candles, rooted in tznius, is itself their publicizing of the miracle. He closes with the Shinever Rav on Eliezer's gift of clothing and a call to strengthen tznius.

en: Kfitzas haderech appears in the Torah only when Eliezer and Yaakov went to find a kallah, because a shidduch is heavenly and not bound by time and space.
The bas kol that announces a match errs repeatedly because a shidduch is too lofty even for a bas kol, which is only a daughter of prophecy.
The tenth utterance of creation, the creation of a partner for man, begins with 'lo tov', reflecting the wrong announcements that come before the right match.
Women were the core of the Chanukah miracle through Yehudis, and so their holiness on Chanukah is greater, shown by their refraining from work while the candles burn.
Women's not lighting their own Chanukah candles, which stems from tznius, is itself a publicizing of the miracle, since tznius was the miracle of Yehudis.

title.en: The sedra of the holy kallos

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens in Yiddish with a reference to the Maggid of Mezritch and the aliyos of the sedra, then says this week's sedra is connected to kallos: it has four holy kallos, Rachel, Leah, Bilhah and Zilpah. He begins to mention two parshiyos with kfitzas haderech and is asked to speak in English.

title.en: Kfitzas haderech only for a kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that the Torah records kfitzas haderech only twice, for Eliezer seeking a kallah for Yitzchak and for Yaakov seeking his own. He explains that this world has two vessels, time and place, which do not apply in Shamayim, and that every chasan and kallah is a new creation.

title.en: Only Hashem makes matches

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Midrash of the queen who tried to pair a thousand servants and failed, and explains that a bas kol announces each match forty days before conception but errs many times first. He tells of the Sanzer Rav, who paid shadchanus even for failed suggestions, and asks why the bas kol makes mistakes at all.

title.en: Why the tenth utterance begins 'lo tov'

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that a shidduch is so heavenly that even a bas kol, a daughter of prophecy, cannot grasp it. He then shows that of the ten utterances of creation, only the tenth, the creation of a partner for man, opens negatively with 'lo tov', reflecting the bas kol's wrong announcements before 'matza isha matza tov'.

title.en: The shadchan's lie and the heavenly match

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tzemach Tzedek that a shidduch must be slightly blemished to come down into this world, which the shadchan's lie accomplishes, and this is why he is paid. For heavenly people like Eliezer's mission no lie is needed, and their journeys, being heavenly, were above time and space through kfitzas haderech. He tells the Neshei that in helping kallos they are partners in the tenth utterance of creation.

title.en: Chanukah, a yom tov of women

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that women are obligated in Chanukah lights though it is time-bound because they were part of the miracle, and that Tosafos brings the Rashbam that they were its core through Yehudis, who saved the Jews from a decree against their tznius. Measuring holiness by the prohibition of work, from Shabbos to Yom Tov to Chol Hamoed, he shows that women's refraining from work while the candles burn reflects their higher kedusha on Chanukah.

title.en: Why women do not light their own candles

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks, with the Chasam Sofer, why women who were the core of the miracle do not light their own candles as mehadrin. The Chasam Sofer answers that the candles were originally lit outside and it was not tznius for women to join the crowd. The Mashgiach asks why the Chashmona'im did not set it inside, and answers that the women's not lighting for the sake of tznius is itself the publicizing of Yehudis's miracle.

title.en: Tznius, Eliezer's gift and Moshiach's light

summary.en: The Mashgiach says he cannot believe a report of immodest dress among the women, and brings the Shinever Rav that Eliezer's gift of clothing to Rivka was a sample of the tznius kept in Avraham's house. He calls Chanukah a time to strengthen tznius, cites the Bnei Yissaschar that the Chanukah lights reveal the light of Moshiach, and closes with blessings to the Neshei.

catalogTitle: קול ה' יחולל אילות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains 'kol Hashem yecholel ayalos' as the last, hardest blow of exile that brings the birth of the geulah, and 'Hashem lamabul yashav' as the flood that turned into the gift of Torah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the seventh 'kol' of Mizmor 29 as the coming of the great Shabbos, when the 'forests' that hide Hashem's kingship are stripped bare and only His glory is heard. He brings the Midrash on the ayalah that cannot give birth until a snake strikes her: so too Klal Yisrael, before the geulah things get worse, as in Egypt when Pharaoh's decree took away the Shabbos rest. With the Chasam Sofer he explains that the beaten shotrim had sacrificed themselves for Shabbos. He brings Rabbi Moshe of Sambor's reading of 'ki ayal ta'arog': the tzaddik forgets his own pain and davens for kavod Shamayim. On 'Hashem lamabul yashav' he says the darkness before Moshiach is like the flood and one must not despair. Through Rashi's Midrash on Matan Torah he explains that rain carries spiritual blessing, and the flood was Torah that came down as gashmiyus. He ends that in the season of tal umatar one davens for the rain of Torah.

en: The seventh 'kol' of Mizmor 29 corresponds to the coming great Shabbos, when the 'forests' that hide Hashem's kingship are stripped away and only His glory is heard in the rebuilt Beis Hamikdash.
Like the ayalah that can only give birth after the snake's blow, Klal Yisrael lacks the strength to bring the geulah, and just before it the exile becomes harder.
Pharaoh's decree was aimed at the Shabbos rest the Jews had won in Egypt, and the shotrim who were beaten for the shortfall were giving their lives for Shabbos.
A tzaddik in his own suffering does not pray for himself but for the honor of Hashem's Name, like the ayalah that forgets her own pains and prays for water for the world.
The present darkness before Moshiach resembles the time of the flood, when Hashem 'sat alone', and just as then He was afterward acknowledged as King forever, so one must not despair now.

Every physical flow from Heaven, such as rain, carries a spiritual flow within it; the flood was Torah that came down in physical form because the generation was unworthy, and at Matan Torah the same flow came down as Torah.

tal umatar as prayer for Torah

title.en: The seventh kol: the great Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the seven 'kolos' of Mizmor 29 parallel the seven days, and reads the seventh, 'kol Hashem yecholel ayalos vayechesof ye'aros', as the coming of the great Shabbos. Then the 'forests', the nations who hide Hashem's kingship like trees hiding the sky, are stripped away, and in the rebuilt Beis Hamikdash only His glory is heard.

title.en: The ayalah, the snake and the birth of the geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Iyov and the Midrash that the ayalah cannot give birth until Hashem sends a snake to strike her. The Midrash's hint is Klal Yisrael, who lack the strength to bring the geulah, so before it comes a blow and the exile grows harder, as in the parsha when Moshe was sent and the bondage became worse.

title.en: Pharaoh's decree against Shabbos and the last blow

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Midrash that the Jews worked at full capacity from the first day, and asks with the Chasam Sofer how the straw decree could add anything. He answers that Moshe had won them a Shabbos rest, which Pharaoh's decree aimed to take away, so the shotrim who were beaten had sacrificed themselves for Shabbos. He then applies the snake's blow to the present, the Holocaust and the worsening exile, as the last tremor before the birth of Moshiach.

title.en: 'Ki ayal ta'arog': praying for kavod Shamayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk 'ki ayal ta'arog al afikei mayim' and the question of Rabbi Moshe of Sambor why it mixes a masculine noun with a feminine verb. He answers that the ayalah in her own birth pains forgets herself and prays for water for the world as if she were a male, and so the tzaddikim in exile pray not for their own troubles but for the honor of Hashem's Name.

title.en: 'Hashem lamabul yashav': do not despair

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the darkest hour before Moshiach, when the world is more lawless than the generation of the flood and it seems Hashem has left it. He reads 'Hashem lamabul yashav' to say that history repeats: at the flood too Hashem sat alone, and afterward 'vayeshev Hashem melech l'olam', so one must not despair.

title.en: Rashi's Midrash and the spirituality within rain

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash cited by Rashi that at Matan Torah the nations, hearing the great sounds, asked Bilam whether Hashem was bringing a flood. To explain it he sets out a principle: every physical flow from Heaven, like rain, carries a spiritual flow, as the Gemara in Taanis says, and the same flow takes different forms, like ice, water and steam.

title.en: Noach, Moshe and the flood as Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the time of the flood was an eis ratzon to give the Torah, and brings the Gemara in Chullin and the Zohar that Noach's soul was Moshe's; because Noach did not pray for his generation the waters are called 'mei Noach', which Moshe repaired with 'mecheini na'. He explains that 'geshem' comes from gashmiyus, that a tzaddik davening for rain means Torah, and that the flood was Torah that came down in physical form and turned to destruction.

title.en: The flood of Torah and davening for tal umatar

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that a Jew in Krias Shema asks for grain, wine and oil of Torah, and explains that the nations' wise men saw in the stars the same arrangement as at the flood; Bilam answered that this time the flood comes as Torah, 'Hashem oz l'amo yiten', a threefold Torah of the shin in 'bashalom'. He closes that in the season of tal umatar a ben Torah should know he is davening for the rain of Torah, and the winter is the time for deep learning.

catalogTitle: הקדמה לפסד"ז

oneLiner.en: Opening his study of Pesukei d'Zimra, the Mashgiach explains that davening is a climb through the worlds to stand before the King, that every word of tefillah is a palace, and that Pesukei d'Zimra cut a path through the angel-filled atmosphere together with Dovid Hamelech.

abstract.en: Having finished the chapters connected to Kabbalas Shabbos, the Mashgiach begins Pesukei d'Zimra. The goal of davening is Shemoneh Esrei, standing before the King, and the way there passes through the four worlds: korbanos, Pesukei d'Zimra, the blessings of Shema, then Shemoneh Esrei. One prepares with mehudar tzitzis and tefillin. Every word of the nusach, composed by the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah with ruach hakodesh, brings a new tikkun each day, so each day's avodah cannot wait for tomorrow. Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, each word is a heichal, a palace; foreign thoughts mean being sent out of it, so one must daven slowly and with effort. The Mashgiach discusses the pace of davening, the merit of guarding the bris, and enduring hardship for Hashem. Pesukei d'Zimra, from the word for cutting, cut through the destructive angels, and what was once optional has become an obligation in our weaker generation.

en: The aim of davening is to reach Shemoneh Esrei and stand before the King, passing on the way through the four worlds that the parts of davening correspond to.
One prepares to stand before the King with proper garments, chiefly tzitzis and tefillin, and the Mashgiach urges getting mehudar ones even when they cost more.
Every word of tefillah was composed with ruach hakodesh so that each day it brings about a different tikkun, since every day and every person has a distinct task.
Each word of davening is a heichal; one must daven with effort and kavanah, saying Pesukei d'Zimra slowly like someone counting coins.
Tefillah is among the things that stand at the height of the world yet people treat lightly, as Dovid Hamelech already testified.
Pesukei d'Zimra cut a way through the atmosphere filled with destructive angels, because whoever goes along with Dovid Hamelech cannot be stopped.
Pesukei d'Zimra were once a voluntary practice of the pious and have become an obligation today, because our generation cannot rise in tefillah without them.

title.en: Davening as a journey to the King

summary.en: The Mashgiach announces that he now begins Pesukei d'Zimra and explains that the goal of davening is Shemoneh Esrei, standing before the King. To get there one passes through the four worlds: korbanos correspond to Asiyah, Pesukei d'Zimra to Yetzirah, the blessings of Shema to Beriah and Shemoneh Esrei to Atzilus.

title.en: Tzitzis and tefillin as royal garments

summary.en: Citing the Zera Kodesh, the Mashgiach says one must prepare proper garments before entering the King, and the chief of these are tzitzis and tefillin, which raise a person and draw the Shechinah upon him. He urges buying mehudar tzitzis made lishmah and fine tefillin, even at extra cost.

title.en: A new tikkun every day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the words of davening, composed by the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah with ruach hakodesh, bring a different tikkun each day, because the world rises daily toward its completion and every person has a unique task. With the Chiddushei HaRim's reading of 'if not now, when', he teaches that today's avodah cannot be pushed off to tomorrow.

title.en: Every word is a heichal

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching, transmitted by the Chasam Sofer, that every word of davening is a heichal guarded by angels, and a foreign thought means being thrown out of it. Dovid Hamelech and the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah had keys to these palaces; Hashem in His mercy admits one who toils, so one must say Pesukei d'Zimra slowly, like counting precious coins.

title.en: How long to daven

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes the poskim's measure of half an hour for Pesukei d'Zimra, tells of tzaddikim and of R' Avraham Ziskind who davened for hours, and of places like Kotzk and Belz where they davened quickly against the yetzer hara, which he says is not for us. He cites the Ba'al HaTanya's middle way and the Gemara's reading of 'kerum zulus livnei adam' as referring to tefillah, which people belittle.

title.en: The one who slays the serpent

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one merits tefillah above all by guarding the bris, and brings the Zohar's mashal that whoever kills the serpent, the yetzer hara, receives the king's daughter, which is tefillah. Since today's street makes it nearly impossible to avoid sin, one must work harder and at least endure davening when it does not come easily.

title.en: Better to be broken before Hashem

summary.en: Every person must pass through suffering; with the Ohr HaChaim on 'mitachas sivlos Mitzrayim', the Mashgiach explains that what one endures for Hashem is taken off other burdens. He brings his rebbe R' Feivel Mitlevitch's reading of 'al tikrei sivro ela shivro': since one must be broken anyway, better to be broken before Hashem, and one who trusts Him gains time for Torah and tefillah.

title.en: Cutting through the angels

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why he starts with Pesukei d'Zimra and, from the Shaarei Orah, describes the atmosphere between earth and heaven as filled with good and destructive angels that let prayers through or block them. 'Zimra' means cutting: by saying the psalms of Dovid Hamelech one goes along with him, and no one can stop him.

title.en: From voluntary practice to obligation

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows from the Gemara that Pesukei d'Zimra were not originally an obligation, though saying them brings great merit, and asks why they are one today. Like the Tzemach Tzedek's answer about later stringencies, and like Maariv that became binding, our generation needs them: when the ketores purified the air prayers could rise, and without it we must say Pesukei d'Zimra. He closes by saying he will begin with Baruch She'amar next time.

catalogTitle: Current Events: The Recession - Give צדקה with שמחה. The קדושים of the Mumbai Massacre

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that a Jew who sees every event, even a recession or the killing of the Mumbai kedoshim, as coming from Hashem for his good will serve Him with simcha, and above all give tzedakah gladly.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Mizmor Lesodah: one who appreciates the hidden miracles Hashem does for him every moment thanks Him in hard times as in good ones, and serves Him with simcha. Citing the Reishis Chochmah that a mitzvah done with simcha weighs a thousand times more, he turns to the poor who interrupt davening: the collector is a messenger bringing a gift that may save the giver. Now that a recession has been announced, the needy are needier than ever and tzedakah matters more. He then speaks of the Mumbai kedoshim, the shluchim who hosted guests in India. Answering why it happened with Hashem's reply to Moshe Rabbeinu about Rabbi Akiva, he brings the Zohar on the place of those killed as Jews, and says they remain on their shlichus before Moshiach. He closes with the hidden miracles of the body, a warning about the dangerous times, and stories of tzaddikim whose joy in mitzvos surpassed every worldly pleasure.

en: One who realizes that every breath and heartbeat is a hidden miracle from Hashem thanks Him for the hard as for the good, and serves Him with simcha.
Following the Reishis Chochmah, the Mashgiach says a mitzvah done with simcha weighs a thousand times more in Heaven, so a dollar given gladly outweighs a hundred given grudgingly.
The poor man who interrupts one's davening is a messenger from Hashem bringing a gift, and the Mashgiach says one should not see him as a disturbance.
In the recession it is harder but more important to give tzedakah, because the needy are needier than ever.
The Mumbai killing must be accepted with the answer Moshe Rabbeinu received about Rabbi Akiva: it is part of Hashem's plan, which will be understood in its time.
According to the Zohar, a Jew killed because he is a Jew goes straight to the heichal of Moshiach, the highest chamber in Gan Eden.
The Mashgiach says the times are dangerous and one must prepare by doing mitzvos, welcoming every small mitzvah as a gift.

title.en: Mizmor Lesodah: thanks for hidden miracles

summary.en: Continuing Mizmor Lesodah, the Mashgiach explains that one who appreciates the hidden miracles Hashem does every moment calls on His name in distress as in salvation, and serves Him with simcha. He brings the Reishis Chochmah that a mitzvah done with simcha weighs a thousand times more.

title.en: The poor man at davening and the recession

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes collectors who interrupt davening and those who give grudgingly, and teaches that each poor man is Hashem's messenger bringing a gift that may save the giver. With a recession announced, he says tzedakah is harder but more important, and the collector should not be seen as a disturbance.

title.en: The Mumbai killing and Hashem's hidden plan

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the Arab terrorists a 'pere adam', tells of the Chofetz Chaim's words to a man moving to Eretz Yisroel after the Tarpat pogroms, and turns to the couple killed in India after hosting many guests. To the question why, he brings Hashem's answer to Moshe Rabbeinu about Rabbi Akiva's death: be silent, this is the plan.

title.en: The place of those killed as Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that a Jew killed for being a Jew goes straight to the heichal of Moshiach and his name is inscribed on Hashem's garment of vengeance. He adds that great tzaddikim longed to die al kiddush Hashem, bringing the Beis Yosef's Maggid Meisharim, where the angel told him he lost that chance through extra wine.

title.en: Shluchim still on their shlichus; the two worms

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the shluchim of the Lubavitcher Rebbe are still on their shlichus, and tells of a talmid of the Ba'al Shem Tov who met Avraham Avinu on the road asking for the redemption; the shluchim should now tell Moshiach the truth about Jews in India. He then tells the parable of the worm in the radish who cannot imagine a strawberry.

title.en: The tzaddik's level and giving with simcha

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a great tzaddik feels the bad is as good as the good, while the Gemara's separate berachos speak to ordinary people. He stresses that he is only repeating what the sefarim demand: simcha and bitachon, and giving the poor man's dollar with simcha, which by the Reishis Chochmah becomes a thousand dollars.

title.en: Miracles of the body and a dangerous world

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the constant hidden miracles of the body, adding that one who never needed rescue has a bigger miracle than those who bring a korban todah. He warns that the world is a barrel of dynamite with a lit wick, brings the Navi's call to seek righteousness, and urges welcoming every small mitzvah, like the dollar for tzedakah, as a gift.

title.en: Stories: the joy of a mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells three stories: Reb Avraham of Ciechanow, who felt more joy putting on tefillin than his friend did winning a lottery; the Kedushas Levi asking whether a luxurious paritz lights Chanukah candles; and a Rebbe who said a paritz sledding on sacks of sugar has no pleasure like his own in saying Nishmas on Shabbos morning.

catalogTitle: לשם יחוד וברוך שאמר

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the l'shem yichud said before Baruch She'amar, as a unification of Hashem with Klal Yisrael done in the name of all Jews, and then the first phrases of Baruch She'amar, showing that creation, Hashem's word and nature itself continue every moment according to the Torah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the l'shem yichud before Pesukei d'Zimra: its aim is to unite Hashem with His Shechinah dwelling in Klal Yisrael, with fear and love as the two wings that lift a mitzvah, and to complete Hashem's Name broken by Amalek. Saying it in the name of all Israel brings the deed into the world of Klal Yisrael, which no accusation reaches, like the Kodesh HaKodashim on Yom Kippur. He then explains it as a moda'ah, a prior declaration that voids later stray thoughts, and tells of the Noda B'Yehuda's teshuva against saying it and the answers to it. Turning to Baruch She'amar, he explains that creation from nothing is renewed every moment, that Hashem is 'gozer u'mekayem' and never changes His mind, and that nature runs according to the Torah, changing as Jews add new chiddushim.

en: The l'shem yichud declares that a mitzvah is done to unite Hashem with His Shechinah in Klal Yisrael, like a groom with a bride, with fear and love.
A mitzvah done in the name of all Israel reaches the root of Klal Yisrael, where no accusation can reach and sins are erased, as on Yom Kippur.
Saying l'shem yichud before a mitzvah works like a moda'ah: a prior declaration that cancels foreign thoughts the yetzer hara may bring in during the mitzvah.
Creation is not a past event: Hashem's ten utterances still act every moment, and without them everything would cease.
'Baruch gozer u'mekayem' means that Hashem, who knows the future, never changes His mind, unlike a human ruler.
Nature runs according to the Torah, so when Jews add new chiddushim in Torah, Hashem renews nature accordingly.

title.en: What l'shem yichud means

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains in simple terms the l'shem yichud said before Baruch She'amar: uniting Hashem with His Shechinah in Klal Yisrael with fear and love, the two wings without which a mitzvah cannot rise, and uniting the letters of Hashem's Name that are split because of Amalek.

title.en: In the name of all Israel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why a mitzvah is done in the name of all Israel: the root world called Klal Yisrael is beyond any accusation, like the Kodesh HaKodashim on Yom Kippur, which is why one must make peace before Yom Kippur and accept ahavas Yisrael before davening.

title.en: L'shem yichud as a moda'ah

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the nusach comes from the early mekubalim and that the Ba'al HaTanya kept it in his siddur only before Baruch She'amar, then explains it as a moda'ah, like the declaration that voids a coerced get, which cancels stray thoughts during a mitzvah.

title.en: The Noda B'Yehuda and the early misnagdim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the first misnagdim were honest people who feared a new movement after the damage of Shabbatai Tzvi, tells of R' Shimon of Yaroslav and the stone-throwing misnaged, and relates that the Noda B'Yehuda wrote a teshuva against saying l'shem yichud, which the Sidduro shel Shabbos refuted; today it is accepted.

title.en: Baruch She'amar: creation renewed every moment

summary.en: The Mashgiach turns to Baruch She'amar, which came down from heaven with eighty-seven words, and explains 'she'amar v'haya ha'olam' and 'omer v'oseh': creation from nothing is not history but goes on every second, shown with the meshalim of a power station's dynamos and a glass held in the hand.

title.en: Gozer u'mekayem: Hashem does not change His mind

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Hashem with politicians who break promises, explains that the One who knows the future cannot change His mind, uses this against religions that claim He gave a new law, grounding it in the mesorah from Sinai, and tells of a Rebbe exiled to Siberia who read 'gozer u'mekayem' about his own survival.

title.en: Oseh bereishis: nature follows the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'oseh bereishis': Hashem looked into the Torah and created the world, so changes in the Torah's psak bring changes in the world, shown from R' Eliezer's town and from R' Chaim Ozer's advice to a sick man to move to Eretz Yisrael, where the Mechaber's ruling holds.

title.en: New chiddushim, new wonders in nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Avnei Nezer healing a sick man through a chiddush in Tosafos, brings that nature changes from generation to generation, and shows that the great flowering of Torah chiddushim in the Acharonim and in our day came together with great wonders in technology.

catalogTitle: ברוך מרחם על הארץ

oneLiner.en: Explaining the blessings 'Baruch merachem al ha'aretz', 'al habriyos', 'meshalem sachar tov' and 'podeh umatzil', the Mashgiach shows that all of creation longs to return to Hashem, that Hashem's mercy and reward are pure kindness, and that above reward and punishment stands Hashem's way of redeeming even the undeserving.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'Baruch merachem al ha'aretz': Hashem has mercy even on the earth, because everything in creation, even plants and lifeless matter, has a longing. The world was built with chesed, which is love, and everything longs to return to its place; a piece of bread longs to be eaten with a brachah, and the hundred daily brachos counter forgetfulness. The earth, lowest of all, longs most to serve Hashem, which is why it is called eretz, from ratzon; the roads to Zion mourn because no pilgrims tread them. Dovid HaMelech too is called eretz. Turning to 'merachem al habriyos', the Mashgiach teaches that a person who shows mercy, like Rebbi with the mouse, arouses mercy above. 'Meshalem sachar tov' praises Hashem for rewarding what no one deserves. Finally, 'podeh umatzil' describes a higher conduct than reward and punishment, seen in Yetzias Mitzrayim, Menashe's teshuvah and the extra verse after the aleph-beis of Tehillim 34.

en: Hashem has mercy even on the earth, because every part of creation, even plants and lifeless matter, has a longing, and above all a longing to return to Hashem.
The earth, the lowest level of creation and furthest from Hashem, has the strongest longing to serve Him; this is why it is called eretz, from ratzon.
A person who has mercy on Hashem's creatures arouses Hashem's mercy on himself, as Rebbi's suffering ended when he had pity on a mouse.
No one can repay Hashem for even one kindness, so all reward He gives, even for refraining from sin, is pure kindness and a praise of Hashem.
Besides the conduct of reward and punishment there is a higher conduct of pidyon, redemption, in which Hashem saves even those who do not deserve it, as a father with his children.
The season from Tu BiShvat until Shavuos is a time of this conduct of pidyon, when the days themselves are days of mercy.

title.en: The longing in all of creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem is merciful even to the earth because everything has a longing, even plants such as date palms, since the world was built with chesed. Everything longs to return to its place; bread longs to be eaten with a brachah, and the hundred daily brachos guard against the forgetfulness that rules up to a hundred.

title.en: Why the earth is called eretz

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Maggid saw fire lift the Ba'al Shem Tov's food to heaven, then explains that the earth, the lowest of creation, longs most to return to Hashem: eretz comes from ratzon. The roads to Zion mourn because pilgrims no longer tread them, so we ask Hashem to have mercy on the earth.

title.en: Dovid HaMelech as eretz; mercy on creatures

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Dovid HaMelech, the last of the ushpizin, is called eretz, and discusses the Beis Yosef's question on the ending of the brachah of Boneh Yerushalayim, answered by Dovid being Yerushalayim. He then turns to 'merachem al habriyos': rain comes in the merit of animals, and he asks how a person merits Hashem's mercy.

title.en: Man's power above; Rebbi and the calf

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares a person to a switch panel whose every act lights up the upper worlds, as with netilas yadayim in the Ramchal's Derech Hashem. He tells the Gemara's story of Rebbi, who suffered after sending away a calf that hid by him and was healed after having mercy on a mouse: mercy below arouses mercy above.

title.en: Meshalem sachar tov: reward as kindness

summary.en: On 'Baruch meshalem sachar tov lirei'av' the Mashgiach brings the Chovos Halevavos and Nishmas: a whole life of mitzvos cannot repay one kindness, even one breath. So any reward is a gift; with the example of a driver who stops at a red light and expects no payment, he shows that Hashem rewards even refraining from sin.

title.en: Podeh umatzil and the season of redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the weeks from Tu BiShvat to Shavuos a rising season full of Yomim Tovim, a time of pidyon. He explains that besides reward and punishment, the conduct of servants, Hashem has a higher conduct with His children, redeeming those who do not deserve it, which is the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy.

title.en: Redemption beyond the rules

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the conduct of pidyon at Yetzias Mitzrayim, when Hashem redeemed the Jews despite the accusation at the Yam Suf, and with Menashe, whose teshuvah Hashem accepted through a tunnel under the Kisei HaKavod. He applies it to the times set for Moshiach that the accuser spoiled, and says that at the time of redemption Hashem will not look at the accuser.

title.en: The verse beyond the aleph-beis

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rav Tzadok: Tehillim 34 and Tehillim 25 follow the aleph-beis, an order of reward and punishment, and each ends with an extra verse of pidyon outside that order. He explains 'nasati chofrecha Mitzrayim' through the angel created by a sin that must find its target, which Hashem sends to a rasha in place of the one doing teshuvah, the secret of kaparos.

catalogTitle: הקל אב הרחמן

oneLiner.en: Moving through Baruch Sheamar to Mizmor LeSodah, the Mashgiach explains that thanking Hashem for every detail of life is the highest praise, the one offering that will remain in the days of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach explains the words of Baruch Sheamar: Ha-Keil speaks of Hashem's bond with all creation, Av of His bond with the Jewish people, and HaRachaman of mercy that does not follow a person's deeds. Each Jew praises Hashem by his own level, and the Mashgiach tells how the Bais Aharon compared a poritz's pleasure to a tzaddik's pleasure in Nishmas. Saying the songs of David HaMelech is a privilege, since David joins in, and he protests a recent public insult to David. He maps the words of Baruch Sheamar onto the whole order of davening, tells of Rabbi Asher's mighty Yechid Chai HaOlamim, and explains why Hashem's name itself is His greatest praise. Mizmor LeSodah comes first, the choicest taste after the brachah, because thanks will outlast all offerings. True hodaah means knowing one received more than his share, and in the end David calls the whole world to praise Hashem.

en: Ha-Keil refers to Hashem's relationship with all creation, Av to His relationship with the Jewish people, and HaRachaman to mercy that is not measured by a person's deeds.
Saying the songs of David HaMelech is a great privilege, since a tzaddik whose words are repeated joins in, so David sings along with those who daven.
Mizmor LeSodah comes right after the brachah of Baruch Sheamar because, like tasting the choicest food after a brachah, it is the most precious of the songs.
One must thank Hashem for every small thing, not only for great events, since every moment of life rests on His constant hashgachah and countless hidden miracles.
True hodaah means recognizing that one has received more than his share, not saying thanks as good manners.
Mizmor LeSodah belongs to the days of Moshiach, when all offerings and prayers will cease except the korban todah and praise of Hashem.

title.en: Ha-Keil, Av HaRachaman, and praise by each one's level

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Ha-Keil as Hashem's bond with all creation and Av HaRachaman as His fatherly mercy toward the Jewish people, not measured by deeds, and discusses the nusach 'hamehulal befi amo'. He explains that chassidim and avadim praise Hashem each by his level, and tells how the Bais Aharon compared a poritz's pleasure ride over sugar to a tzaddik's pleasure in saying Nishmas.

title.en: Singing together with David HaMelech

summary.en: On 'uveshirei Dovid avdecha', the Mashgiach explains that David's soul is the greatest, and since a tzaddik's lips move in the grave when his words are repeated, David sings along with us. He protests a recent public insult to David HaMelech in Eretz Yisrael and says a Jew should sing David's songs all the more with pride and joy.

title.en: From shevachos to Yechid Chai HaOlamim

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows how the words of Baruch Sheamar point to the whole order of davening, from Mizmor LeSodah through Shemoneh Esrei, and explains Yechid Chai HaOlamim. He tells how Rabbi Asher's Yechid Chai HaOlamim was heard a mile away, and explains why, unlike a king, Hashem's own name is His greatest praise.

title.en: Why Mizmor LeSodah comes first

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mizmor LeSodah was composed for the korban todah, which is why it is omitted on Erev Pesach and Erev Yom Kippur. It comes first after the brachah like the choicest fruit after a brachah, or the tasting of Shabbos food on Erev Shabbos, and it belongs to the days of Moshiach when only the todah will remain.

title.en: Thanks that can never suffice

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls thanks the most important bond between a creation and his Creator, bringing Nishmas to show that no praise is enough even for one kindness. He cites the Mishnah Berurah that kavanah is needed at Modim as at Avos, and says one must accustom himself to praise Hashem for every small thing, for every breath.

title.en: Hashgachah in every detail of the body

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yesod VeShoresh HaAvodah, who thanked Hashem even for finding his snuff box, and says a person who stumbles should first thank Hashem, since Hashem watches each person like a baby. He describes the countless parts of the body that could fail at any moment, cites 'ein ba'al haneis makir beniso', and brings the Tomer Devorah that Hashem gives strength even to one who sins.

title.en: Hodaah, Yehudah and the end of days

summary.en: From 've'ish lefi mehalelo' the Mashgiach explains that a person is measured by his praise of Hashem, which is why kingship came from Yehudah, named for Leah's thanks. Following Rashi, true hodaah is knowing one took more than his share, as Yaakov said 'katonti'. He then brings Chazal that only the todah will remain, R. Samson Raphael Hirsch that Mizmor LeSodah closes Moshe Rabbeinu's eleven psalms, and notes it is the hundredth psalm.

title.en: Hari'u: a tzaddik's word moves the world

summary.en: On 'hari'u laShem kol ha'aretz' the Mashgiach explains, with the Nefesh HaChaim, that man is the soul of the world, so a tzaddik like David can awaken all mankind to praise Hashem. He brings Rashi and the Ramban on the sign 'pakod pakadti' and an answer that words entering the heart are the sign of the redeemer, and argues that the Rambam's Moshiach, who needs no signs, is greater, since one word of his will move all of Klal Yisrael.

catalogTitle: Current Events: Conquering the Fear of our Times With אמונה

oneLiner.en: Speaking impromptu as war with Iraq looms, the Mashgiach explains that the troubles before Moshiach can come as fear alone, that Hashem runs events hidden as in the Megillah, and that the answer to the fear is bitachon.

abstract.en: Asked to speak about current events, the Mashgiach begins with Chazal's chevlei Moshiach, the birth pains before the redemption, and shows they need not be harsh: Mitzrayim lasted 210 years instead of 400, and tzaddikim said the Holocaust could have been worse. The pain can come as fear alone. He explains the double hiding, hester b'soch hester, that the Torah foretells, with a mashal of a son who does not even know his father is near. The fear today comes from Yishmael, worst of the oppressors, a 'pere adam' no one can reason with. Adar, the end of the year, mirrors the end of time: its miracles, like the Megillah's, are cloaked in nature, and every event today is part of a Megillah being written. The Torah commands bitachon, and one who trusts Hashem breaks the hester panim. He closes with Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, a world without clear leadership, and the strength of a double Adar.

en: The Mashgiach explains that chevlei Moshiach need not be physical suffering; Klal Yisrael can go through them with fear alone.
Before Moshiach there is hester b'soch hester: Hashem is hidden and the hiding itself is hidden.
Like the events of the Megillah, everything happening today is part of Hashem's hidden plan to help the Jewish people.
The Torah commands bitachon, and one who relies on Hashem sees that Hashem takes care of him and breaks through the hester panim.
Real bitachon is a lifelong work that must be practiced until it becomes second nature.
Before Moshiach the Jewish people are left without leaders who can say with certainty what Hashem wants, so they must rely on Hashem alone.

title.en: Chevlei Moshiach can come as fear

summary.en: Speaking without preparation, the Mashgiach compares the coming of Moshiach to a birth with its pains, and shows from Mitzrayim, the Rebbe Reb Elimelech and the Holocaust that the pains need not be harsh. He says the discomfort can come as fear alone, and that we seem to be in the era of ikvesa d'Meshicha.

title.en: Hester b'soch hester: the double hiding

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Vayelech that Hashem will hide His face before the end, and why tzaddikim no longer show open wonders. He explains the double hiding with a mashal of a hunter's son who does not even know his father is near, and cites the Ba'al Shem Tov's fear of this state.

title.en: The four kingdoms and Yishmael

summary.en: Turning to the looming war with Iraq, the Mashgiach goes through the four kingdoms that oppressed the Jews since the first churban, up to Edom in which we still are, and says the Midrashim and the Rambam describe the trouble from Yishmael before Moshiach as the worst. He repeats that this trouble can come as fear.

title.en: Adar, the end of time, and hidden miracles

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the year is a miniature of all time: Nisan is revealed miracles, and Adar, its end, is miracles cloaked in nature. In the Megillah Hashem's name never appears and the miracles are a chain of small incidents, yet 'the King' and even Achashveirosh allude to Hashem who directs everything.

title.en: A Megillah being written today

summary.en: With a mashal of bochurim in the days of Achashveirosh who brushed off the news about Vashti, the Mashgiach says everything world leaders say and do today is part of a Megillah. As with Haman's decree, the trouble may stay a fear, and the fear comes from Yishmael, a 'pere adam' with whom one cannot reason, unlike earlier oppressors.

title.en: The mitzvah of bitachon

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the answer to the fear is bitachon, a mitzvah rooted in the first of the Aseres HaDibros. One who tells Hashem that he relies on Him sees Hashem's care and breaks the hester panim, and his bitachon helps all of Klal Yisrael. He brings Shoshanas Yaakov and the Steipler sitting by his window during the Gulf War.

title.en: Practicing bitachon; a chain of rescues

summary.en: The Mashgiach says real bitachon takes a lifetime of practice, but one must start now. He tells of a Jewish soldier saved by saying Shema, says the survivors of the Holocaust will not suffer a second such blow, and recounts how Russia fell apart just before the Gulf War, part of a chain of miracles since the Holocaust.

title.en: No leaders, no fear, and the strength of Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges not to fear but to learn, daven and give tzedakah, and explains that before Moshiach the Jews are left without leaders who can tell them Hashem's word, so they must rely on Hashem. He asks that the fear fall on the goyim as Haman's decree turned on him, and closes with the Gemara that Adar is a time of victory, doubled this year.

catalogTitle: מזמור לתודה - עניני שמחה ואמונה

oneLiner.en: On Mizmor L'Sodah, the Mashgiach explains that serving Hashem with simcha grows out of clear emunah and bitachon, the very thing Amalek attacks with doubt, and that only such joyful service survives a test.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues with the second verse of Mizmor L'Sodah, 'Ivdu es Hashem b'simcha', and ties simcha to emunah. Amalek, whose name equals safek (doubt) in gematria, wages constant war on Jewish faith, and in this polluted, lowest generation, like Adar, the lowest month, doubts come easily. Simcha is the opposite of doubt: the one with clear emunah and bitachon is joyful, as a poor young man showed with his 'two cows', two verses of trust. The Megillah teaches that nothing is chance. The tochacha came because Hashem was served without simcha, and routine Judaism collapsed at the first test in America. The Ruzhiner's story shows learning every word of Gemara as holy. 'Hu asanu v'lo anachnu' teaches that Hashem makes a person and guides His people like a shepherd. Entering with thanks leads to tehillah, and a hundred brachos with amen strengthen emunah.

en: Serving Hashem with simcha depends on emunah: simcha is the security of a person who has no doubts, while doubt is Amalek's weapon.
The Megillah, which never mentions Hashem's name, teaches that every event is guided by hashgacha pratis and nothing happens by chance.
Judaism kept only out of routine and tradition, without simcha, does not withstand a test, as seen in the immigrants who worked on Shabbos in America.
'Hu asanu v'lo anachnu' means that Hashem, not a person's own wisdom or effort, makes him and his success.
One who enters Hashem's gates with thanks, even for the smallest step, merits to enter His courtyards with tehillah, a higher level.
The hundred daily brachos, answered with amen, are the 'hundred gates' through which a person enters emunah and draws down blessing.

title.en: Simcha rests on emunah; Amalek's war on faith

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'Ivdu es Hashem b'simcha' and says simcha comes from emunah, which Amalek constantly fights by casting doubts. He compares the spiritual pollution of the world to its physical pollution and says this is why doubts enter Jewish minds so easily today, though they are only a test to be fought.

title.en: Adar, the lowest month, and the end of exile

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Amalek counted Adar as his month: as the last month it corresponds to the last, lowest generations, the heel before Moshiach. He compares the end of the Babylonian exile, when Achashverosh celebrated because seventy years had seemingly passed, to today, and notes that Amalek equals safek in gematria.

title.en: Simcha as certainty: the two cows and the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one with clear emunah and bitachon is joyful, and tells of a poor young man whose 'two cows' were two verses of trust. He then explains that the Megillah, where Hashem's name is not even mentioned, teaches that nothing is mikreh (chance), the claim of Amalek, and that simcha is the opposite of doubt.

title.en: Without simcha, routine fails the test

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Reb Chaim Vital that the Arizal reached his revelations through simcha, and the verse at the end of the tochacha that it came because Hashem was not served with simcha. He explains that service out of routine collapses at a test, as with immigrants to America who worked on Shabbos and whose descendants lost everything Jewish, and calls for chiyus in davening and learning.

title.en: The Ruzhiner and every word of Gemara

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Ruzhiner remembered which Amora said a teaching when a scholar did not, explaining that for him 'amar Rava' was also part of the holy Gemara. He concludes that learning is the living word of Hashem instructing a person, and the test of service not done out of tradition is whether it is done with simcha.

title.en: 'Hu asanu v'lo anachnu': Hashem makes us

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'Elokim' as the master of all forces, as at Eliyahu's confrontation with the Baal, and 'hu asanu v'lo anachnu' as rejecting the idea of 'making a living' or a self-made career, which he compares to Pharaoh's boast. With Rashi he explains that Hashem made us before we existed, fixing a person's talents, match and livelihood before birth.

title.en: His people and His flock, even against the enemies

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that whatever Haman, Amalek, Hitler or today's antisemites claim, the Jews are Hashem's people. He contrasts the Zionist hope that a land would end antisemitism, relating a prediction of Reb Chaim via Rav Sorotzkin, with the certainty that Hashem runs history, and reads 'v'lo' with a vav and the shepherd of Tehillim 23 as assurance.

title.en: Entering with thanks, then with tehillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Jew of real emunah who rejoices at being able to stand a test, and explains 'bo'u she'arav b'sodah': one should enter shul, the beis medrash and Shabbos thanking Hashem for being let in, as an old Stoliner chassid taught. Through thanks for even the smallest step one reaches the courtyards 'bis'hilah', a higher praise, as Ashrei begins with Tehillah L'Dovid.

title.en: A hundred brachos, a hundred gates of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the sefarim that 'she'arav' are the hundred daily brachos, parallel to the hundred sockets of the Mishkan, and explains that one hundred is the domain of the Samech-Mem, while 101 goes beyond it. A brachah is complete with amen, and through the amens, 'shomer emunim', one enters the hundred gates and draws down blessing.

catalogTitle: המשך מזמור לתודה - עניני שמחה ואמונה

oneLiner.en: Continuing Mizmor l'Sodah, the Mashgiach explains Adar as the hidden, lowest month in which Hashem's name is incomplete, how answering amen and amen yehei shmei rabbah restores it, and why the test of the last generations is emunah alone.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach returns to Mizmor l'Sodah and explains that, just as souls and places have a 'head' and a 'heel', Adar is the heel among the months: a month of concealment, like Persia (Eilam) and the Megillah, where Hashem's name does not appear. He brings the Gemara that answering amen yehei shmei rabbah with all one's strength tears up a decree of seventy years, and Tosafos' reading that it is a prayer for the incomplete name, hidden by Amalek and Haman, to become whole. Answering amen, from emunah, opens the hundred gates, and Mizmor l'Sodah, the hundredth psalm, enters them with thanks. He explains why Chanukah and Purim belong to Modim, tells of the souls who were told the remedy is emunah, shows the Megillah's chain of hidden miracles, and ends with guarding emunah from today's media and strengthening it through Torah.

en: Adar is the 'heel' of the months, a month of hiddenness like Eilam (Persia), where miracles are concealed in nature and Hashem's name does not appear in the Megillah.
Amen yehei shmei rabbah is a prayer that Hashem's name, made incomplete by Amalek and Haman's concealment, become whole, and Adar is a special time to put strength into it.
Answering amen, which comes from emunah, opens the hundred gates of heaven; Mizmor l'Sodah, the hundredth psalm, corresponds to the last of them and enters with thanks.
Chanukah and Purim, weekday festivals made for the galus, are mentioned in Modim, where one bows down, because the Shechinah comes down to the lowest places and the lowest Jews.
For the last generations the remedy is emunah alone; the whole matter of Purim is believing in Hashem and in hashgacha pratis.
Guarding emunah has two sides: avoiding literature and media that plant doubts, and strengthening it through deep, warm learning of Torah.

title.en: Adar, the hidden heel of the months

summary.en: Resuming Mizmor l'Sodah, the Mashgiach explains from Sefer Yetzirah that place, time and soul each have a head and a heel: Nissan is the head and Adar the heel. Adar is like Eilam (Persia), a place of concealment, the time of Esther and hester panim, when Hashem's name is hidden in the Megillah.

title.en: Amen yehei shmei rabbah and the incomplete name

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that answering amen yehei shmei rabbah with all one's strength tears up a seventy-year decree, and links it to the end of the seventy years of galus Bavel under Persia. Through Tosafos and Rashi on 'ki yad al kes Yah' he explains that Amalek and Haman hide Hashem's name, and the prayer asks that it become whole.

title.en: Amen opens the hundred gates

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that amen means from beginning to end of all levels, and that whoever is careful with amen has all the gates opened for him, reading 'pischu she'arim' as the nation that answers amen. Amen comes from emunah, and Mizmor l'Sodah, the hundredth psalm, corresponds to the last of the hundred gates and enters them with thanks.

title.en: Hoda'ah, Modim and the weekday festivals

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains hoda'ah as thanks for more than one's share, from Leah naming Yehudah, and calls Kislev and Adar months of hoda'ah. Torah festivals appear in Retzeh, the avodah of the Beis Hamikdash, while Chanukah and Purim, weekday festivals made for galus, appear in Modim where one bows down. He describes Jews on the levels of Shabbos, Yom Tov and Chol Hamoed.

title.en: Melacha as a curse; the Shechinah comes down

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that melacha is a curse: Adam before the sin did no work, and the thirty-nine curses became the thirty-nine melachos, which is why Shabbos, a source of blessing, has none. He lays out the levels of Jews by how much work they do, and explains that on Chanukah and Purim the Shechinah comes down to the lowest place, like a great man visiting the sick.

title.en: The souls told the remedy is emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties Adar to the heel before Moshiach and to the prayer for a whole name, and brings Chavakuk, who set all the mitzvos on 'tzaddik be'emunaso yichyeh'. He retells the story of a great disciple of the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples: souls who kept returning in gilgulim with a failing mark went up level by level to Hashem, who told them the remedy is emunah.

title.en: Purim is emunah: the chain of hidden miracles

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the whole matter of Purim is emunah and hashgacha pratis: every detail of the Megillah, from Vashti to Mordechai and Bigsan and Teresh, fits into one plan beyond chance, as the meforshim such as the Alshich and the Nesivos show. A person who wrote down his own life would see the same chain, as the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo says.

title.en: Purim's seriousness and thanks for every detail

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Adar is the time to strengthen emunah and to learn the Megillah with its meforshim, and brings the Chasam Sofer against treating Purim as frivolity: Purim is an awesome day like Yom Kippur. With a mashal of a president caring about every detail of a simple man's day, he explains the thanks of Modim for a life in Hashem's hand, and 'ki tov Hashem le'olam chasdo'.

title.en: Emunah down the generations; the Rambam's warning

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'ad dor vador emunaso' as emunah tumbling down to the lowest generations until Moshiach, and says the test of our time is emunah, as the Chofetz Chaim said about a dybbuk. Guarding emunah has a sur mera and an aseh tov; for the first he brings the Rambam forbidding books that plant doubts, and asks why the precise Rambam adds 'many books'.

title.en: Today's media, and emunah through Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that 'many books' includes all literature: newspapers, television and even radio news fill the mind with filth and doubts in emunah. For aseh tov he explains that deep, warm Torah learning shows its wonders and that it is from heaven, and preparing for Purim through it builds emunah. Where the ghetto once preserved Jews, today in free America they must mix and still hold on to emunah.

catalogTitle: הקדמה לאשרי. בכל יום אברכך

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why Ashrei is so great a praise: Hashem feeds every creature in a perfectly balanced order, He is a personal G-d who fills every small need, and each day He gives a new blessing.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that whoever says Tehillah l'David three times a day is assured of the World to Come, because it is arranged by the alef-beis and contains 'Pose'ach es yadecha'. He asks what is so wonderful about feeding all creatures, and answers that only habit hides the wonder: every creature gets its own food, and all of nature is held in a precise balance, which the alef-beis order hints at. He then explains why we first say 'Ashrei yoshvei veisecha': one must settle oneself before davening. A story of the Toldos Yaakov Yosef and Eliyahu Hanavi teaches 'ashrei ha'am shekachah lo' as accepting everything as hashgachah pratis. He explains 'Elokai haMelech' as two relationships, the general King and the personal G-d, and 'bechol yom avarcheka' as giving Hashem strength to bestow good, new every day and every Shabbos.

en: Only habit keeps people from seeing the wonder that every creature in the world receives its own food in its own place.
The alef-beis order of Ashrei hints at the precise order and balance with which Hashem provides parnassah to all of creation.
Before davening one must sit and settle one's mind, and after davening not run off; this is why Tehillah l'David is preceded by 'Ashrei yoshvei veisecha'.
'Elokai haMelech' expresses two relationships with Hashem: the King of the whole world, and one's personal G-d to whom one turns for every small thing.
Every day and every Shabbos brings a new blessing and new tikkunim; nothing in davening is a repetition.

candidateTopics: parnassah and the balance of nature
Hashem as personal G-d and King

title.en: Why Ashrei earns the World to Come

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one who says Tehillah l'David three times daily is a ben olam haba, because of its alef-beis and 'Pose'ach es yadecha'. He asks what is so great about feeding all creatures when people and animals sometimes die of hunger.

title.en: The wonder hidden by habit

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that we take for granted what would amaze us if it happened once in a lifetime, like the sunrise. Every creature gets its own food, animals prepare for winter, and only a famine makes headlines; he brings the Chasam Sofer on the generation of the desert seeing bread grow from the ground.

title.en: Hunger as a decree; nature's balance

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when someone dies of hunger it is a specific decree from Heaven, like any illness, while the general order is that every creature has food. He describes how worms, birds and birds of prey keep each other in proportion, a balance unchanged for thousands of years that only man can disturb.

title.en: Parnassah with an alef-beis

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that this is the meaning of Ashrei: each creature desires its own food, which serves several purposes in its habitat, and the alef-beis signifies that parnassah comes with order. Tehillah l'David is a song of amazement, and one who contemplates it three times a day rather than by rote is a ben olam haba.

title.en: Settling the mind before davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Tehillah l'David is preceded by 'Ashrei yoshvei veisecha': the Gemara says the early chassidim waited an hour before and after davening, learning it from this pasuk and from 'yeshvu yesharim es panecha'. He adds that one should begin with simchah and security in Hashem, and that 'Ashrei' is the foremost of the expressions of praise in Tehillim.

title.en: The Toldos and 'zol zain azoi'

summary.en: After explaining the second Ashrei, 'Ashrei ha'am shekachah lo', the Mashgiach tells how the Toldos Yaakov Yosef, upset at not being waited for at a bris, saw a guest answer everything with 'zol zain azoi'. It was revealed to be Eliyahu Hanavi teaching him that everything is hashgachah pratis, and the Toldos explained the pasuk accordingly.

title.en: Elokai haMelech: two relationships

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'tehillah' is a very high level of praise and translates 'Aromimcha'. 'HaMelech' is Hashem as the general King, like a president one would not ask for bananas, while 'Elokai' is the personal G-d one turns to for everything; he illustrates with Reb Nachum of Chernobyl praying that a maid should not leave.

title.en: Elokai written full: no empty space

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that 'Elokai' here is written full, with a vav, meaning there is no empty space in a person's life that is not Hashem's concern, down to a toothpick after a meal. 'Va'avarchah shimcha l'olam va'ed' means that through this praise one merits praising Hashem in the World to Come.

title.en: Bechol yom avarcheka: a new blessing daily

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'avarcheka' truly means blessing Hashem, giving Him strength to bestow good, as in Rabbi Yishmael's blessing in the Kodesh Hakodashim. Every day has its own blessing and tikkun, as the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah built the prayers to carry new meanings each day; he brings the Shelah's 600,000 Shabbosos, each Jew having his own Shabbos and his own letter in the Torah.

catalogTitle: ברכת החמה: The Revelation that the Power of the Sun Belongs to יעקב

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the sun, now harnessed to Esav and the order of nature, returns every 28 years to its point of origin, when it belongs to Yaakov and is blessed in Birkas HaChamah, and that this year's Birkas HaChamah on Erev Pesach carries great hope for the geulah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rashi's teaching that Yaakov and Esav are never up together, and shows it in Yerushalayim, usually spelled without its second yud while Rome stands. Hashem gave the red sun to Esav and the white moon to Yaakov, yet in truth everything was created for Yisrael; the sun is only harnessed to Esav's wagon of nature until Moshiach. Esav merely mimics Yaakov; he is a mirage, and one of his aliases is chametz, so burning chametz is destroying Amalek. The Mashgiach then develops a law of return: everything goes back to its root, as in yovel, where a Jew returns to the fiftieth level above nature. Nature has 28 levels, the 28 times of Koheles, and the sun, king of nature, returns to its first point every 28 years; then it belongs to Yaakov and is blessed. Falling on Erev Pesach, this Birkas HaChamah signals great hopes. He closes by urging joyful acceptance of Hashem's will, even if clouds prevent the brachah.

en: Yaakov and Esav are like two sides of a seesaw: when one rises the other falls, so Hashem gave the sun to Esav and the moon to Yaakov.
In truth everything, the sun included, belongs to Yisrael; the sun is only harnessed now to Esav's wagon of nature, and when Moshiach comes both sun and moon will belong to Yaakov.
Everything in creation must return to its root; yovel is the return of a Jew to his root, the fiftieth level, which is above nature.
The sun, king of nature, returns every 28 years to the exact point where it stood at creation on the fourth day, and only then, when it belongs to Yaakov, is a brachah made over it.
Birkas HaChamah on Erev Pesach, the morning of burning chametz, is an especially strong return to the root, tied to the tradition that the wiping out of Amalek will be on Erev Pesach.
The Mashgiach says a person should try to serve Hashem as best he can, but when circumstances do not follow his plan he should accept it with joy, even if clouds keep him from making the brachah.

candidateTopics: yovel and the return to the root

title.en: Yaakov and Esav on a seesaw; sun and moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Yaakov and Esav are never up together, as Tzor filled up from the ruin of Yerushalayim, and explains why Yerushalayim is usually written without its second yud while Rome exists. He then explains that the red sun was given to Esav and the white moon to Yaakov, which is why Yisrael counts by the moon.

title.en: The sun truly belongs to Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from Rashi that the world was created for Yisrael, so the sun too belongs to them, and is now only harnessed to Esav's wagon of nature. When Moshiach comes both lights will belong to Yaakov, who holds Esav's heel; Esav only mimics Yaakov and is in truth a mirage.

title.en: Chametz, Esav's alias

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Esav has many names, one of them chametz, so burning chametz on Erev Pesach destroys Amalek. He distinguishes chametz from machmetzes, the leaven that spreads it, bringing the Or HaChaim's dream of fighting the male and female forces of evil, where the female was stronger, and contrasts the nations' 'ladies first' with the Jewish way of right over left.

title.en: The law of return and the yovel

summary.en: The Mashgiach lays down a 'law of return': everything must go back to its root, as Koheles describes the cycle of water. He shows it in yovel, when the eved returns to his family, in Yetzias Mitzrayim as the Ramban explains, and in the fiftieth level, which is above the seven-by-seven of nature.

title.en: The sun's yovel every 28 years

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that nature has 28 levels, the 28 times of Koheles and the 28 letters of the Torah's first passuk, and that the sun, king of nature, returns every 28 years to the point where it was placed on the fourth day. This is the sun's yovel, and then, when it belongs to Yaakov, a brachah is made over it.

title.en: Birkas HaChamah on Erev Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when the sun's return falls on Erev Pesach it is far stronger, because of the tradition that Amalek will be wiped out on Erev Pesach and the Gemara's concern that the Beis HaMikdash may be built on Pesach. Time itself returns to its origin, the first 'time to be born', and the coming of Moshiach is a birth; he calls on every Jew to make a reckoning of how he can be reborn.

title.en: Like an infant with its mother

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Dovid HaMelech's comparison of himself to an infant with its mother and tells of a chassid whose Rebbe wrote 'sometimes do the opposite' beside each line of his daily schedule. He applies this to Birkas HaChamah: prepare fully, but if clouds prevent the brachah, accept it with joy, knowing that Jews around the world are saying it.

catalogTitle: גדול ה' ומהלל מאד

oneLiner.en: On the words of Ashrei, 'Gadol Hashem… v'ligdulaso ein cheker', the Mashgiach explains that Hashem cannot be grasped by investigation but is known through the neshamah, the mesorah of Sinai, the tzaddikim of every generation and the beauty of His world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the verse 'Gadol Hashem u'mehulal me'od, v'ligdulaso ein cheker' and explains that each sense grasps its own kind of thing, and the intellect is not the faculty that grasps Hashem. Every Jew has a neshamah and a measure of ruach hakodesh, blocked only by sin; Klal Yisroel as a whole has it, which is why its minhagim are true, as the Binas Adam and Rav Moshe Feinstein show. The human mind was made for the physical world; Hashem is felt through Torah, mitzvos and kedushah. The Torah never proves the ikkarim by investigation: they rest on what an entire nation saw at Sinai, as the Yismach Moshe writes. On 'dor l'dor yeshabach ma'asecha' he explains that the tzaddikim of each generation reveal Hashem, with stories of Lechovitch, Belz and the Satmar Rav's megillah, and that later generations understand Hashem's ways. He ends with 'hadar kevod hodecha': the grace and beauty of creation.

en: Each sense grasps its own kind of thing, and the intellect with its investigation is not the faculty through which a person grasps Hashem.
Every Jew has a neshamah that is a part of G-d and a potential for ruach hakodesh; sin insulates him from it, and Klal Yisroel as a whole has ruach hakodesh, so its minhagim are true.
The human mind was made only for the physical world; Hashem is felt through Torah, mitzvos, honesty and kedushah, not through calculation.

The Torah never brings proofs from investigation for its foundations; Jewish belief rests on the experience of an entire nation at Yetzias Mitzrayim and Sinai, handed down from generation to generation.
'Dor l'dor yeshabach ma'asecha': the tzaddikim of each generation are Hashem's handiwork, through whom His praise is told.
What one generation cannot understand of Hashem's ways becomes clear to later generations, as with the rebuilding of Torah after the destruction in Europe.
'Hadar kevod hodecha': Hashem made the world with grace and beauty beyond what was needed, and for this one must thank and praise Him.
